techniques.name: Data Obfuscation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.

procedures.text: StrelaStealer encrypts the payload of HTTP POST communications using the same XOR key used for the malware's DLL payload.
Gamaredon Group has used obfuscated VBScripts with randomly generated variable names and concatenated strings.
Okrum leverages the HTTP protocol for C2 communication, while hiding the actual messages in the Cookie and Set-Cookie headers of the HTTP requests.
SystemBC has encoded with XOR and encrypted with RC4 its beacon.

techniques.name: Junk Data
techniques.summary: Adversaries may add junk data to protocols used for command and control to make detection more difficult.

procedures.text: P2P ZeuS added junk data to outgoing UDP packets to peer implants.
Downdelph inserts pseudo-random characters between each original character during encoding of C2 network requests, making it difficult to write signatures on them.
Mori has obfuscated the FML.dll with 200MB of junk data.
LODEINFO can append C2 communication with randomly generated junk data.

techniques.name: Steganography
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use steganographic techniques to hide command and control traffic to make detection efforts more difficult.

procedures.text: LunarWeb can receive C2 commands hidden in the structure of .jpg and .gif images.
Axiom has used steganography to hide its C2 communications.
HAMMERTOSS is controlled via commands that are appended to image files.
Sliver can encode binary data into a .PNG file for C2 communication.

techniques.name: Protocol or Service Impersonation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may impersonate legitimate protocols or web service traffic to disguise command and control activity and thwart analysis efforts.

procedures.text: Lazarus Group malware also uses a unique form of communication encryption known as FakeTLS that mimics TLS but uses a different encryption method, potentially evading SSL traffic inspection/decryption.
FRAMESTING uses a cookie named `DSID` to mimic the name of a cookie used by Ivanti Connect Secure appliances for maintaining VPN sessions.

StarProxy has utilized TLS record headers in network packets to impersonate various versions of TLS protocols to blend in with legitimate network traffic. StarProxy used FakeTLS to communicate with its C2 server.

PUBLOAD has modified HTTP POST requests to resemble legitimate communications. PUBLOAD used FakeTLS headers in network packets to impersonate various versions of TLS protocols to blend in with legitimate network traffic. PUBLOAD has util...

techniques.name: OS Credential Dumping
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material, normally in the form of a hash or a clear text password.

procedures.text: Ember Bear gathers credential material from target systems, such as SSH keys, to facilitate access to victim environments.
APT39 has used different versions of Mimikatz to obtain credentials.
Carbanak obtains Windows logon password details.
MgBot includes modules for dumping and capturing credentials from process memory.

techniques.name: LSASS Memory
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS).

procedures.text: Indrik Spider used Cobalt Strike to carry out credential dumping using ProcDump.
OilRig has used credential dumping tools such as Mimikatz to steal credentials to accounts logged into the compromised system and to Outlook Web Access.
Cleaver has been known to dump credentials using Mimikatz and Windows Credential Editor.
Leafminer used several tools for retrieving login and password information, including LaZagne and Mimikatz.

techniques.name: Security Account Manager
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to extract credential material from the Security Account Manager (SAM) database either through in-memory techniques or through the Windows Registry where the SAM database is stored.

procedures.text: Daggerfly used Reg to dump the Security Account Manager (SAM) hive from victim machines for follow-on credential extraction.
CrackMapExec can dump usernames and hashed passwords from the SAM.
gsecdump can dump Windows password hashes from the SAM.
GALLIUM used reg commands to dump specific hives from the Windows Registry, such as the SAM hive, and obtain password hashes.

techniques.name: NTDS
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to access or create a copy of the Active Directory domain database in order to steal credential information, as well as obtain other information about domain members such as devices, users, and...

procedures.text: APT28 has used the ntdsutil.exe utility to export the Active Directory database for credential access.
CrackMapExec can dump hashed passwords associated with Active Directory using Windows' Directory Replication Services API (DRSUAPI), or Volume Shadow Copy.
Scattered Spider has extracted the `NTDS.dit` file by creating volume shadow copies of virtual domain controller disks.
Sandworm Team has used `ntdsutil.exe` to back up the Active Directory database, likely for credential access.

techniques.name: LSA Secrets
techniques.summary: Adversaries with SYSTEM access to a host may attempt to access Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, which can contain a variety of different credential materials, such as credentials for service accounts.

procedures.text: MuddyWater has performed credential dumping with LaZagne.

IceApple's Credential Dumper module can dump LSA secrets from registry keys, including: `HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\PolEKList\default`, `HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets\\CurrVal`, and `HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets\\OldVal`.
CosmicDuke collects LSA secrets.
gsecdump can dump LSA secrets.

techniques.name: Cached Domain Credentials
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to access cached domain credentials used to allow authentication to occur in the event a domain controller is unavailable.

procedures.text: Okrum was seen using modified Quarks PwDump to perform credential dumping.
APT33 has used a variety of publicly available tools like LaZagne to gather credentials.
Leafminer used several tools for retrieving login and password information, including LaZagne.
Cachedump can extract cached password hashes from cache entry information.

techniques.name: DCSync
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to access credentials and other sensitive information by abusing a Windows Domain Controller's application programming interface (API) to simulate the replication process from a remote domain c...

procedures.text: Mimikatz performs credential dumping to obtain account and password information useful in gaining access to additional systems and enterprise network resources. It contains functionality to acquire information about credentials in many w...
Earth Lusca has used a DCSync command with Mimikatz to retrieve credentials from an exploited controller.
Mustang Panda has leveraged Mimikatz DCSync feature to obtain user credentials.
Storm-0501 has utilized DCSync to extract credentials from victims.

techniques.name: Proc Filesystem
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather credentials from the proc filesystem or `/proc`. The proc filesystem is a pseudo-filesystem used as an interface to kernel data structures for Linux based systems managing virtual memory.

procedures.text: Mini Shai-Hulud has scraped runner process memory to extract short-lived identity tokens, which it then exchanged for per-package npm trusted-publisher tokens.
PACEMAKER has the ability to extract credentials from OS memory.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can scrape memory from the Runner.Worker process by reading `/proc/ /mem` to extract secrets including plaintext tokens.
LaZagne can use the ` /maps` and ` /mem` files to identify regex patterns to dump cleartext passwords from the browser's process memory.

techniques.name: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to dump the contents of /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow to enable offline password cracking.

procedures.text: LaZagne can obtain credential information from /etc/shadow using the shadow.py module.

techniques.name: Data from Local System
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search local system sources, such as file systems, configuration files, local databases, virtual machine files, or process memory, to find files of interest and sensitive data prior to Exfiltration.

procedures.text: Troll Stealer gathers information from infected systems such as SSH information from the victim's `.ssh` directory. Troll Stealer collects information from local FileZilla installations and Microsoft Sticky Note.

Kimsuky has collected Office, PDF, and HWP documents from its victims. Kimsuky has also harvested victim files through the use of the `RecentFiles()` function that collects paths of recently accessed files by parsing .lnk shortcuts from...
BRONZE BUTLER has exfiltrated files stolen from local systems.
Proxysvc searches the local system and gathers data.

techniques.name: Direct Volume Access
techniques.summary: Adversaries may directly access a volume to bypass file access controls and file system monitoring. Windows allows programs to have direct access to logical volumes.

procedures.text: esentutl can use the Volume Shadow Copy service to copy locked files such as `ntds.dit`.
Scattered Spider has created volume shadow copies of virtual domain controller disks to extract the `NTDS.dit` file.
Volt Typhoon has executed the Windows-native `vssadmin` command to create volume shadow copies.

techniques.name: System Service Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may try to gather information about registered local system services.

procedures.text: Ursnif has gathered information about running services.
BRONZE BUTLER has used TROJ_GETVERSION to discover system services.
Sykipot may use net start to display running services.
Comnie runs the command: net start >> %TEMP%\info.dat on a victim.

techniques.name: Fallback Channels
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use fallback or alternate communication channels if the primary channel is compromised or inaccessible in order to maintain reliable command and control and to avoid data transfer thresholds.

procedures.text: DEEPROOT has communicated with multiple C2 servers as a means of redundancy if one fails.

JHUHUGIT tests if it can reach its C2 server by first attempting a direct connection, and if it fails, obtaining proxy settings and sending the connection through a proxy, and finally injecting code into a running browser if the proxy me...
Linfo creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can change C2 servers.
CHOPSTICK can switch to a new C2 channel if the current one is broken.

techniques.name: Application Window Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of open application windows. Window listings could convey information about how the system is used.

procedures.text: Attor can obtain application window titles and then determines which windows to perform Screen Capture on.
NetTraveler reports window names along with keylogger information to provide application context.
Cadelspy has the ability to identify open windows on the compromised host.
Flagpro can check the name of the window displayed on the system.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a different network medium than the command and control channel.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Bluetooth
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over Bluetooth rather than the command and control channel.

procedures.text: Flame has a module named BeetleJuice that contains Bluetooth functionality that may be used in different ways, including transmitting encoded information from the infected system over the Bluetooth protocol, acting as a Bluetooth beacon,...

techniques.name: Query Registry
techniques.summary: Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry to gather information about the system, configuration, and installed software.

procedures.text: Epic uses the rem reg query command to obtain values from Registry keys.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate Registry items.
Sibot has queried the registry for proxy server information.
FatDuke can get user agent strings for the default browser from HKCU\Software\Classes\http\shell\open\command .

techniques.name: Rootkit
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use rootkits to hide the presence of programs, files, network connections, services, drivers, and other system components.

procedures.text: Ebury acts as a user land rootkit using the SSH service.
Winnti Group used a rootkit to modify typical server functionality.
APT41 deployed rootkits on Linux systems.
Rocke has modified /etc/ld.so.preload to hook libc functions in order to hide the installed dropper and mining software in process lists.

techniques.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may look for details about the network configuration and settings, such as IP and/or MAC addresses, of systems they access or through information discovery of remote systems.

procedures.text: Explosive has collected the MAC address from the victim's machine.
Chrommme can enumerate the IP address of a compromised host.
ifconfig can be used to display adapter configuration on Unix systems, including information for TCP/IP, DNS, and DHCP.
HEXANE has used Ping and `tracert` for network discovery.

techniques.name: Internet Connection Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may check for Internet connectivity on compromised systems.

procedures.text: GoldFinder performed HTTP GET requests to check internet connectivity and identify HTTP proxy servers and other redirectors that an HTTP request traveled through.
More_eggs has used HTTP GET requests to check internet connectivity.
Neoichor can check for Internet connectivity by contacting bing[.]com with the request format `bing[.]com?id= `.
Magic Hound has conducted a network call out to a specific website as part of their initial discovery activity.

techniques.name: Wi-Fi Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search for information about Wi-Fi networks, such as network names and passwords, on compromised systems.

procedures.text: Magic Hound has collected names and passwords of all Wi-Fi networks to which a device has previously connected.
PUBLOAD has collected information on Wi-Fi networks from victim hosts leveraging `netsh wlan show profiles`, `netsh wlan show interface`, and `netsh wlan show`.
CharmPower can use `netsh wlan show profiles` to list specific Wi-Fi profile details.
Machete uses the netsh wlan show networks mode=bssid and netsh wlan show interfaces commands to list all nearby WiFi networks and connected interfaces.

techniques.name: Remote System Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of other systems by IP address, hostname, or other logical identifier on a network that may be used for Lateral Movement from the current system.

procedures.text: Ember Bear has used tools such as Nmap and MASSCAN for remote service discovery.
menuPass uses scripts to enumerate IP ranges on the victim network. menuPass has also issued the command net view /domain to a PlugX implant to gather information about remote systems on the network.
MURKYTOP has the capability to identify remote hosts on connected networks.
The TAINTEDSCRIBE command and execution module can perform target system enumeration.

techniques.name: Automated Exfiltration
techniques.summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data, such as sensitive documents, through the use of automated processing after being gathered during Collection.

procedures.text: StrongPity can automatically exfiltrate collected documents to the C2 server.
Kimsuky has exfiltrated data to C2 servers using an automated script that executes every 10 minutes and after successful checks for the presence of pre-designated staged filenames.
LightNeuron can be configured to automatically exfiltrate files under a specified directory.
Sidewinder has configured tools to automatically send collected files to attacker controlled servers.

techniques.name: Traffic Duplication
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage traffic mirroring in order to automate data exfiltration over compromised infrastructure. Traffic mirroring is a native feature for some devices, often used for network analysis.

procedures.text: Salt Typhoon has enabled traffic mirroring to exfiltrate data.

techniques.name: Remote Services
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a service that accepts remote connections, such as telnet, SSH, and VNC. The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

procedures.text: Wizard Spider has used the WebDAV protocol to execute Ryuk payloads hosted on network file shares.
MacMa can manage remote screen sessions.
Brute Ratel C4 has the ability to use RPC for lateral movement.
Kivars has the ability to remotely trigger keyboard input and mouse clicks.

techniques.name: Remote Desktop Protocol
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a computer using the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

procedures.text: Kimsuky has used RDP for direct remote point-and-click access.
INC Ransom has used RDP to move laterally.
Cobalt Strike can start a VNC-based remote desktop server and tunnel the connection through the already established C2 channel.
QuasarRAT has a module for performing remote desktop access.

techniques.name: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with a remote network share using Server Message Block (SMB). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

procedures.text: Conti can spread via SMB and encrypts files on different hosts, potentially compromising an entire network.
Moses Staff has used batch scripts that can enable SMB on a compromised host.
Threat Group-1314 actors mapped network drives using net use .
HermeticWizard can use a list of hardcoded credentials to to authenticate via NTLMSSP to the SMB shares on remote systems.

techniques.name: Distributed Component Object Model
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote machines by taking advantage of Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM).

procedures.text: Empire can utilize Invoke-DCOM to leverage remote COM execution for lateral movement.
SILENTTRINITY can use `System` namespace methods to execute lateral movement using DCOM.
Cobalt Strike can deliver Beacon payloads for lateral movement by leveraging remote COM execution.

techniques.name: SSH
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into remote machines using Secure Shell (SSH). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

procedures.text: FIN7 has used SSH to move laterally through victim environments.
Lazarus Group used SSH and the PuTTy PSCP utility to gain access to a restricted segment of a compromised network.
Leviathan used ssh for internal reconnaissance.
Scattered Spider has used SSH to move laterally in victim environments and to access the vSphere vCenter Server GUI.

techniques.name: VNC
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to remotely control machines using Virtual Network Computing (VNC).

procedures.text: ZxShell supports functionality for VNC sessions.
Gamaredon Group has used VNC tools, including UltraVNC, to remotely interact with compromised hosts.
FIN7 has used TightVNC to control compromised hosts.
DanBot can use VNC for remote access to targeted systems.

techniques.name: Windows Remote Management
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote systems using Windows Remote Management (WinRM). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

procedures.text: FIN13 has leveraged `WMI` to move laterally within a compromised network via application servers and SQL servers.
Brute Ratel C4 can use WinRM for pivoting.
Chimera has used WinRM for lateral movement.
Storm-0501 has utilized the post-exploitation tool known as Evil-WinRM that uses PowerShell over Windows Remote Management (WinRM) for remote code execution.

techniques.name: Cloud Services
techniques.summary: Adversaries may log into accessible cloud services within a compromised environment using Valid Accounts that are synchronized with or federated to on-premises user identities.

procedures.text: Storm-0501 has used compromised Entra Connect Sync Server to move laterally within the victim environment.
Mini Shai-Hulud has accessed and propagated to AWS EC2 instances via SSM Send-Command.
APT29 has leveraged compromised high-privileged on-premises accounts synced to Office 365 to move laterally into a cloud environment, including through the use of Azure AD PowerShell.
Scattered Spider has also leveraged pre-existing AWS EC2 instances for lateral movement and data collection purposes.

techniques.name: Direct Cloud VM Connections
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage Valid Accounts to log directly into accessible cloud hosted compute infrastructure through cloud native methods.

techniques.name: Data from Removable Media
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search connected removable media on computers they have compromised to find files of interest.

procedures.text: Once a removable media device is inserted back into the first victim, USBStealer collects data from it that was exfiltrated from a second victim.
InvisiMole can collect jpeg files from connected MTP devices.
Aria-body has the ability to collect data from USB devices.
OilRig has used Wireshark’s usbcapcmd utility to capture USB traffic.

techniques.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents on the system or in transit.

procedures.text: Shai-Hulud has utilized double-base64 encoding to store stolen secrets within the Github Action Logs within the victim account. Shai-Hulud has also leveraged three layers of base64 encoding of exfiltrated data for anti-forensic purposes.
BackdoorDiplomacy has obfuscated tools and malware it uses with VMProtect.
Sliver obfuscates configuration and other static files using native Go libraries such as `garble` and `gobfuscate` to inhibit configuration analysis and static detection.
Ryuk can use anti-disassembly and code transformation obfuscation techniques.

techniques.name: Binary Padding
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use binary padding to add junk data and change the on-disk representation of malware.

procedures.text: TAINTEDSCRIBE can execute FileRecvWriteRand to append random bytes to the end of a file received from C2.
Emotet inflates malicious files and malware as an evasion technique.
Javali can use large obfuscated libraries to hinder detection and analysis.
QakBot can use large file sizes to evade detection.

techniques.name: Software Packing
techniques.summary: Adversaries may perform software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code. Software packing is a method of compressing or encrypting an executable.

procedures.text: The Gentlemen has packed The Gentlemen Ransomware binaries utilizing either Themida or Enigma to obfuscate the malicious payloads.
GoldMax has been packed for obfuscation.
Lokibot has used several packing methods for obfuscation.
Cuba has a packed payload when delivered.

techniques.name: Steganography
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use steganography techniques in order to prevent the detection of hidden information.

procedures.text: TeamPCP has hidden malicious payloads in the frame data of WAV audio files.
Earth Lusca has used steganography to hide shellcode in a BMP image file.
RDAT can also embed data within a BMP image prior to exfiltration.
PowerDuke uses steganography to hide backdoors in PNG files, which are also encrypted using the Tiny Encryption Algorithm (TEA).

techniques.name: Compile After Delivery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code.

procedures.text: Gamaredon Group has compiled the source code for a downloader directly on the infected system using the built-in Microsoft.CSharp.CSharpCodeProvider class.
Sliver includes functionality to retrieve source code and compile locally prior to execution in victim environments.
FoggyWeb can compile and execute source code sent to the compromised AD FS server via a specific HTTP POST.
Rocke has compiled malware, delivered to victims as .c files, with the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC).

techniques.name: Indicator Removal from Tools
techniques.summary: Adversaries may remove indicators from tools if they believe their malicious tool was detected, quarantined, or otherwise curtailed.

procedures.text: UNC3886 has replaced atomic indicators mentioned in threat intelligence publications, sometimes as quickly as under a week after release.
The author of GravityRAT submitted samples to VirusTotal for testing, showing that the author modified the code to try to hide the DDE object in a different part of the document.
Cobalt Strike includes a capability to modify the Beacon payload to eliminate known signatures or unpacking methods.
Patchwork apparently altered NDiskMonitor samples by adding four bytes of random letters in a likely attempt to change the file hashes.

techniques.name: HTML Smuggling
techniques.summary: Adversaries may smuggle data and files past content filters by hiding malicious payloads inside of seemingly benign HTML files.

procedures.text: QakBot has been delivered in ZIP files via HTML smuggling.
APT29 has embedded an ISO file within an HTML attachment that contained JavaScript code to initiate malware execution.
EnvyScout contains JavaScript code that can extract an encoded blob from its HTML body and write it to disk.

techniques.name: Dynamic API Resolution
techniques.summary: Adversaries may obfuscate then dynamically resolve API functions called by their malware in order to conceal malicious functionalities and impair defensive analysis.

procedures.text: Mustang Panda has leveraged obfuscated Windows API function calls that were concealed as unique names, or hashes of the Windows API.
SplatDropper has leveraged hashed Windows API calls using a seed value of "131313".
TONESHELL has utilized a modified DJB2 algorithm to resolve APIs.
Kimsuky has leveraged dynamic API resolution using custom hashing techniques.

techniques.name: Stripped Payloads
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to make a payload difficult to analyze by removing symbols, strings, and other human readable information.

procedures.text: macOS.OSAMiner has used run-only Applescripts, a compiled and stripped version of AppleScript, to remove human readable indicators to evade detection.
Cuckoo Stealer is a stripped binary payload.

techniques.name: Embedded Payloads
techniques.summary: Adversaries may embed payloads within other files to conceal malicious content from defenses.

procedures.text: Moneybird contains a configuration blob embedded in the malware itself.
The DEADEYE.EMBED variant of DEADEYE has the ability to embed payloads inside of a compiled binary.
Lazarus Group has distributed malicious payloads embedded in PNG files.
BADHATCH has an embedded second stage DLL payload within the first stage of the malware.

techniques.name: Command Obfuscation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may obfuscate content during command execution to impede detection. Command-line obfuscation is a method of making strings and patterns within commands and scripts more difficult to signature and analyze.

procedures.text: Aquatic Panda has encoded PowerShell commands in Base64.
Sardonic PowerShell scripts can be encrypted with RC4 and compressed using Gzip.
Sandworm Team has used ROT13 encoding, AES encryption and compression with the zlib library for their Python-based backdoor.
HEXANE has used Base64-encoded scripts.

techniques.name: Fileless Storage
techniques.summary: Adversaries may store data in "fileless" formats to conceal malicious activity from defenses. Fileless storage can be broadly defined as any format other than a file.

procedures.text: DarkWatchman can store configuration strings, keylogger, and output of components in the Registry.
PolyglotDuke can store encrypted JSON configuration files in the Registry.
QakBot can store its configuration information in a randomly named subkey under HKCU\Software\Microsoft .

TYPEFRAME can install and store encrypted configuration data under the Registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\ShellCompatibility\Applications\laxhost.dll and HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Window...

techniques.name: LNK Icon Smuggling
techniques.summary: Adversaries may smuggle commands to download malicious payloads past content filters by hiding them within otherwise seemingly benign windows shortcut files.

procedures.text: Kimsuky has used the LNK icon location to execute malicious scripts. Kimsuky has also padded the LNK target field properties with extra spaces to obscure the script.
Gamaredon Group has used LNK files to hide malicious scripts for execution.
TONESHELL has been initiated using LNK files that were programmed to display a PDF icon to entice the victim to click on the file to execute an office.exe binary.

Mustang Panda has utilized LNK files to hide malicious scripts for execution. Mustang Panda has also leveraged LNK files that were programmed to display a PDF icon to entice the victim to click on the file to execute an office.exe binary.

techniques.name: Encrypted/Encoded File
techniques.summary: Adversaries may encrypt or encode files to obfuscate strings, bytes, and other specific patterns to impede detection.

procedures.text: DEADEYE has encrypted its payload.
Qilin can employ several code obfuscation methods, including renaming functions, altering control flows, and encrypting strings.
Torisma has been Base64 encoded and AES encrypted.
OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D encrypts its strings in RSA256 and encodes them in a custom base64 scheme and XOR.

techniques.name: Polymorphic Code
techniques.summary: Adversaries may utilize polymorphic code (also known as metamorphic or mutating code) to evade detection. Polymorphic code is a type of software capable of changing its runtime footprint during code execution.

procedures.text: BendyBear changes its runtime footprint during code execution to evade signature-based defenses.

techniques.name: Compression
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files.

procedures.text: Pony attachments have been delivered via compressed archive files.
DarkWatchman has been delivered as compressed RAR payloads in ZIP files to victims.
Hancitor has delivered compressed payloads in ZIP files to victims.
RTM has been delivered to targets as various archive files including ZIP, 7-ZIP, and RAR.

techniques.name: Junk Code Insertion
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use junk code / dead code to obfuscate a malware’s functionality. Junk code is code that either does not execute, or if it does execute, does not change the functionality of the code.

procedures.text: Maze has inserted large blocks of junk code, including some components to decrypt strings and other important information for later in the encryption process.
A version of XTunnel introduced in July 2015 inserted junk code into the binary in a likely attempt to obfuscate it and bypass security products.
StrelaStealer variants have included excessive mathematical functions padding the binary and slowing execution for anti-analysis and sandbox evasion purposes.
MiniJunk has been compiled through several obfuscation techniques to include junk code insertion.

techniques.name: SVG Smuggling
techniques.summary: Adversaries may smuggle data and files past content filters by hiding malicious payloads inside of seemingly benign SVG files.

techniques.name: Invisible Unicode
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse invisible or non-printing Unicode characters to conceal malicious content within files, scripts, or text.

procedures.text: GlassWorm has utilized invisible Unicode Private Use Area (PUA) characters to obfuscate its malicious code so that it does not render in code editors.

techniques.name: Scheduled Transfer
techniques.summary: Adversaries may schedule data exfiltration to be performed only at certain times of day or at certain intervals. This could be done to blend traffic patterns with normal activity or availability.

procedures.text: jRAT can be configured to reconnect at certain intervals.
Flagpro has the ability to wait for a specified time interval between communicating with and executing commands from C2.
Shark can pause C2 communications for a specified time.
LightNeuron can be configured to exfiltrate data during nighttime or working hours.

techniques.name: Data Transfer Size Limits
techniques.summary: An adversary may exfiltrate data in fixed size chunks instead of whole files or limit packet sizes below certain thresholds.

procedures.text: Play has split victims' files into chunks for exfiltration.
LuminousMoth has split archived files into multiple parts to bypass a 5MB limit.
Threat Group-3390 actors have split RAR files for exfiltration into parts.
OopsIE exfiltrates command output and collected files to its C2 server in 1500-byte blocks.

techniques.name: System Owner/User Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to identify the primary user, currently logged in user, set of users that commonly uses a system, or whether a user is actively using the system.

procedures.text: Trojan.Karagany can gather information about the user on a compromised host.
PoetRAT sent username, computer name, and the previously generated UUID in reply to a "who" command from C2.
Revenge RAT gathers the username from the system.
DRATzarus can obtain a list of users from an infected machine.

techniques.name: Masquerading
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools.

procedures.text: menuPass has used esentutl to change file extensions to their true type that were masquerading as .txt files.
APT32 has disguised a Cobalt Strike beacon as a Flash Installer.

Contagious Interview has delivered BeaverTail malware masquerading as legitimate software or applications. Contagious Interview has also delivered malicious payloads masquerading as legitimate software drivers.
Pony has used the Adobe Reader icon for the downloaded file to look more trustworthy.

techniques.name: Invalid Code Signature
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to mimic features of valid code signatures to increase the chance of deceiving a user, analyst, or tool.

procedures.text: WindTail has been incompletely signed with revoked certificates.
BADNEWS is sometimes signed with an invalid Authenticode certificate in an apparent effort to make it look more legitimate.
Regin stage 1 modules for 64-bit systems have been found to be signed with fake certificates masquerading as originating from Microsoft Corporation and Broadcom Corporation.
APT37 has signed its malware with an invalid digital certificates listed as “Tencent Technology (Shenzhen) Company Limited.”

techniques.name: Right-to-Left Override
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse the right-to-left override (RTLO or RLO) character (U+202E) to disguise a string and/or file name to make it appear benign.

procedures.text: Ferocious Kitten has used right-to-left override to reverse executables’ names to make them appear to have different file extensions, rather than their real ones.
BlackTech has used right-to-left-override to obfuscate the filenames of malicious e-mail attachments.
Ke3chang has used the right-to-left override character in spearphishing attachment names to trick targets into executing .scr and .exe files.
Scarlet Mimic has used the left-to-right override character in self-extracting RAR archive spearphishing attachment file names.

techniques.name: Rename Legitimate Utilities
techniques.summary: Adversaries may rename legitimate / system utilities to try to evade security mechanisms concerning the usage of those utilities.

procedures.text: PHASEJAM has renamed the file `/home/bin/remotedebug` to `remotedebug.bak`, allowing the threats actors to write a malicious `/home/bin/remotedebug` shell script.
StrelaStealer has used a renamed, legitimate `msinfo32.exe` executable to sideload the StrelaStealer payload during initial installation.
menuPass has renamed certutil and moved it to a different location on the system to avoid detection based on use of the tool.
Lazarus Group has renamed system utilities such as wscript.exe and mshta.exe .

techniques.name: Masquerade Task or Service
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate the name of a task or service to make it appear legitimate or benign. Tasks/services executed by the Task Scheduler or systemd will typically be given a name and/or description.

procedures.text: NIMBUS MANTICORE has masqueraded as legitimate services.
DCSrv has masqueraded its service as a legitimate svchost.exe process.
In one instance, menuPass added PlugX as a service with a display name of "Corel Writing Tools Utility."
Aquatic Panda created new, malicious services using names such as Windows User Service to attempt to blend in with legitimate items on victim systems.

techniques.name: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
techniques.summary: Adversaries may match or approximate the name or location of legitimate files, Registry keys, or other resources when naming/placing them.

procedures.text: Misdat saves itself as a file named `msdtc.exe`, which is also the name of the legitimate Microsoft Distributed Transaction Coordinator service binary.
DCSYNCER.SLICK has stored stolen credentials in legitimate resource locations to include `C:\Program Files\VMware\VMwareTools\VMwareVGAuth\LOG.txt`.
RainyDay has used names to mimic legitimate software including "vmtoolsd.exe" to spoof Vmtools.
TeamTNT has replaced .dockerd and .dockerenv with their own scripts and cryptocurrency mining software.

techniques.name: Space after Filename
techniques.summary: Adversaries can hide a program's true filetype by changing the extension of a file.

procedures.text: APT38 has put several spaces before a file extension to avoid detection and suspicion.
Keydnap puts a space after a false .jpg extension so that execution actually goes through the Terminal.app program.

techniques.name: Double File Extension
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse a double extension in the filename as a means of masquerading the true file type.

procedures.text: DarkGate masquerades malicious LNK files as PDF objects using the double extension .pdf.lnk .
The Bazar loader has used dual-extension executable files such as PreviewReport.DOC.exe.
Kimsuky has used an additional filename extension to hide the true file type. Kimsuky has also masqueraded malicious LNK files as PDF objects using the double extension .pdf.lnk.
Mustang Panda has used an additional filename extension to hide the true file type.

techniques.name: Masquerade File Type
techniques.summary: Adversaries may masquerade malicious payloads as legitimate files through changes to the payload's formatting, including the file’s signature, extension, icon, and contents.

procedures.text: HeartCrypt can append a BMP header to encoded malicious payloads to masquerade them as BMP files.
Volt Typhoon has appended copies of the ntds.dit database with a .gif file extension.
Kapeka masquerades as a Microsoft Word Add-In file, with the extension `.wll`, but is a malicious DLL file.
BlackByte masqueraded configuration files containing encryption keys as PNG files.

techniques.name: Break Process Trees
techniques.summary: An adversary may attempt to evade process tree-based analysis by modifying executed malware's parent process ID (PPID).

procedures.text: After initial execution, BPFDoor forks itself and runs the fork with the `--init` flag, which allows it to execute secondary clean up operations. The parent process terminates leaving the forked process to be inherited by the legitimate...
Shai-Hulud has augmented its installation process by having its original install process exit cleanly to provide the user with the illusion that the service is installed normally.

techniques.name: Masquerade Account Name
techniques.summary: Adversaries may match or approximate the names of legitimate accounts to make newly created ones appear benign. This will typically occur during Create Account, although accounts may also be renamed at a later date.

procedures.text: Flame can create backdoor accounts with login `HelpAssistant` on domain connected systems if appropriate rights are available.
Storm-1811 has created Microsoft Teams accounts that spoof IT support and helpdesk members for use in application and voice phishing.
Magic Hound has created local accounts named `help` and `DefaultAccount` on compromised machines.
Dragonfly has created accounts disguised as legitimate backup and service accounts as well as an email administration account.

techniques.name: Overwrite Process Arguments
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify a process's in-memory arguments to change its name in order to appear as a legitimate or benign process.

procedures.text: BPFDoor overwrites the `argv[0]` value used by the Linux `/proc` filesystem to determine the command line and command name to display for each process. BPFDoor selects a name from 10 hardcoded names that resemble Linux system daemons, su...

techniques.name: Browser Fingerprint
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to blend in with legitimate traffic by spoofing browser and system attributes like operating system, system language, platform, user-agent string, resolution, time zone, etc.

procedures.text: FatDuke has attempted to mimic a compromised user's traffic by using the same user agent as the installed browser.
LIGHTRAIL has leveraged hard-coded User Agent strings to mimic legitimate browser traffic.

MiniFast has blended into network traffic by mimicking a Chrome browser using the following User-Agent string: `Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/146.0.0.0 Safari/537.36`.

techniques.name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use scripts automatically executed at boot or logon initialization to establish persistence.

procedures.text: SPAWNCHIMERA has modified the boot process files within `/tmp/coreboot_fs/bin/init` to establish persistence.
APT41 used a hidden shell script in `/etc/rc.d/init.d` to leverage the `ADORE.XSEC`backdoor and `Adore-NG` rootkit.
APT29 has hijacked legitimate application-specific startup scripts to enable malware to execute on system startup.
Depending on the Linux distribution and when executing with root permissions, RotaJakiro may install persistence using a `.conf` file in the `/etc/init/` folder.

techniques.name: Logon Script (Windows)
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use Windows logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence. Windows allows logon scripts to be run whenever a specific user or group of users log into a system.

procedures.text: An APT28 loader Trojan adds the Registry key HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript to establish persistence.
Attor's dispatcher can establish persistence via adding a Registry key with a logon script HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Environment "UserInitMprLogonScript" .
JHUHUGIT has registered a Windows shell script under the Registry key HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript to establish persistence.
KGH_SPY has the ability to set the HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript Registry key to execute logon scripts.

techniques.name: Login Hook
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use a Login Hook to establish persistence executed upon user logon. A login hook is a plist file that points to a specific script to execute with root privileges upon user logon.

techniques.name: Network Logon Script
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use network logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence. Network logon scripts can be assigned using Active Directory or Group Policy Objects.

procedures.text: The Gentlemen Ransomware has utilized the domain’s NETLOGON share to distribute the malicious payload to all domain-joined systems.

techniques.name: RC Scripts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence by modifying RC scripts, which are executed during a Unix-like system’s startup.

procedures.text: Velvet Ant used a modified `/etc/rc.local` file on compromised F5 BIG-IP devices to maintain persistence.
HiddenWasp installs reboot persistence by adding itself to /etc/rc.local .
The Gentlemen Ransomware has utilized RC scripts to establish persistence in ESXi service.
UNC3886 has placed a bash installation script into `/etc/rc.local.d/` to establish persistence.

techniques.name: Startup Items
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use startup items automatically executed at boot initialization to establish persistence.

procedures.text: jRAT can list and manage startup entries.

techniques.name: Data from Network Shared Drive
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search network shares on computers they have compromised to find files of interest.

procedures.text: RedCurl has collected data about network drives.
CosmicDuke steals user files from network shared drives with file extensions and keywords that match a predefined list.
APT28 has collected files from network shared drives.
Gamaredon Group malware has collected Microsoft Office documents from mapped network drives.

techniques.name: Network Sniffing
techniques.summary: Adversaries may passively sniff network traffic to capture information about an environment, including authentication material passed over the network.

procedures.text: Sandworm Team has used intercepter-NG to sniff passwords in network traffic.
Kimsuky has used the Nirsoft SniffPass network sniffer to obtain passwords sent over non-secure protocols.
Impacket can be used to sniff network traffic via an interface or raw socket.
NBTscan can dump and print whole packet content.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
techniques.summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an existing command and control channel. Stolen data is encoded into the normal communications channel using the same protocol as command and control communications.

procedures.text: OilBooster can use an actor-controlled OneDrive account for C2 communication and exfiltration.
MechaFlounder has the ability to send the compromised user's account name and hostname within a URL to C2.
LAMEHUG can exfiltrate collected system information and documents to C2.
PoetRAT has exfiltrated data over the C2 channel.

techniques.name: Network Service Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of services running on remote hosts and local network infrastructure devices, including those that may be vulnerable to remote software exploitation.

procedures.text: Pupy has a built-in module for port scanning.
Volt Typhoon has used commercial tools, LOTL utilities, and appliances already present on the system for network service discovery.
APT39 has used CrackMapExec and a custom port scanner known as BLUETORCH for network scanning.
BlackTech has used the SNScan tool to find other potential targets on victim networks.

techniques.name: Windows Management Instrumentation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to execute malicious commands and payloads. WMI is designed for programmers and is the infrastructure for management data and operations on Windows systems.

procedures.text: Sardonic can use WMI to execute PowerShell commands on a compromised machine.
Meteor can use `wmic.exe` as part of its effort to delete shadow copies.
Cinnamon Tempest has used Impacket for lateral movement via WMI.
RogueRobin uses various WMI queries to check if the sample is running in a sandbox.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
techniques.summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a different protocol than that of the existing command and control channel.

procedures.text: Bundlore uses the curl -s -L -o command to exfiltrate archived data to a URL.
PoetRAT has used a .NET tool named dog.exe to exiltrate information over an e-mail account.
Play has used WinSCP to exfiltrate data to actor-controlled accounts.
TeamTNT has sent locally staged files with collected credentials to C2 servers using cURL.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
techniques.summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a symmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
techniques.summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an asymmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

procedures.text: APT28 has exfiltrated archives of collected data previously staged on a target's OWA server via HTTPS.
IcedID has exfiltrated collected data via HTTPS.
BRUSHFIRE has the ability to exfiltrate data on-demand through executing commands obtained via monitoring for specially crafted packets and sending output back in an embedded SSL response.
CURIUM has used SMTPS to exfiltrate collected data from victims.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
techniques.summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an un-encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

procedures.text: Lazarus Group malware SierraBravo-Two generates an email message via SMTP containing information about newly infected victims.
FIN8 has used FTP to exfiltrate collected data.
Remsec can exfiltrate data via a DNS tunnel or email, separately from its C2 channel.
CookieMiner has used the curl --upload-file command to exfiltrate data over HTTP.

techniques.name: System Network Connections Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of network connections to or from the compromised system they are currently accessing or from remote systems by querying for information over the network.

procedures.text: Lucifer can identify the IP and port numbers for all remote connections from the compromised host.
Trojan.Karagany can use netstat to collect a list of network connections.
Babuk can use “WNetOpenEnumW” and “WNetEnumResourceW” to enumerate files in network resources for encryption.
APT38 installed a port monitoring tool, MAPMAKER, to print the active TCP connections on the local system.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data via a physical medium, such as a removable drive.

techniques.name: Exfiltration over USB
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a USB connected physical device. In certain circumstances, such as an air-gapped network compromise, exfiltration could occur via a USB device introduced by a user.

procedures.text: SPACESHIP copies staged data to removable drives when they are inserted into the system.
Remsec contains a module to move data from airgapped networks to Internet-connected systems by using a removable USB device.
USBStealer exfiltrates collected files via removable media from air-gapped victims.
Tropic Trooper has exfiltrated data using USB storage devices.

techniques.name: Scheduled Task/Job
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

procedures.text: Lokibot's second stage DLL has set a timer using “timeSetEvent” to schedule its next execution.

techniques.name: At
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse the at utility to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

procedures.text: Threat Group-3390 actors use at to schedule tasks to run self-extracting RAR archives, which install HTTPBrowser or PlugX on other victims on a network.
CrackMapExec can set a scheduled task on the target system to execute commands remotely using at.
APT18 actors used the native at Windows task scheduler tool to use scheduled tasks for execution on a victim network.
BRONZE BUTLER has used at to register a scheduled task to execute malware during lateral movement.

techniques.name: Cron
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse the cron utility to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. The cron utility is a time-based job scheduler for Unix-like operating systems.

procedures.text: The Gentlemen Ransomware has leveraged `crontab` to launch the ransomware after a 60-second delay upon reboot using `echo '@reboot sleep 60 && /bin/.vmware-authd ' | crontab - 2>/dev/null`.
SpeakUp uses cron tasks to ensure persistence.
Anchor can install itself as a cron job.
Janicab used a cron job for persistence on Mac devices.

techniques.name: Scheduled Task
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

procedures.text: GoldMax has used scheduled tasks to maintain persistence.
SystemBC has executed a copy of itself as a scheduled task with the `start` command. The copy of SystemBC has random file and directory names within the ProgramData directory.
JSS Loader has the ability to launch scheduled tasks to establish persistence.
BabyShark has used scheduled tasks to maintain persistence.

techniques.name: Systemd Timers
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse systemd timers to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. Systemd timers are unit files with file extension .timer that control services.

procedures.text: APT38 has used a multiplatform implant that can write to `~/.config/systemd/nvmconf/` to gain persistence on Linux hosts.

Mini Shai-Hulud has obtained persistence on Linux devices by writing the `gh-token-monitor` daemon within `~/.config/systemd/user/gh-token-monitor.service` that polls GitHub every 60 seconds. Mini Shai-Hulud has also leveraged a daemon c...
CanisterWorm has registered itself as a systemd service for persistence on targeted Kubernetes nodes.

techniques.name: Container Orchestration Job
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality provided by container orchestration tools such as Kubernetes to schedule deployment of containers configured to execute malicious code.

techniques.name: Process Injection
techniques.summary: Adversaries may inject code into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

procedures.text: NOOPLDR can inject decrypted payloads into processes including wuauclt.exe., rdrleakdiag.exe, and tabcal.exe.
APT38 has injected malicious payloads into the `explorer.exe` process. APT38 has also injected malicious binaries directly into memory on compromised hosts.
Agent Tesla can inject into known, vulnerable binaries on targeted hosts.
Lizar can migrate the loader into another process.

techniques.name: Dynamic-link Library Injection
techniques.summary: Adversaries may inject dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

procedures.text: Heyoka Backdoor can inject a DLL into rundll32.exe for execution.
Saint Bot has injected its DLL component into `EhStorAurhn.exe`.
Emissary injects its DLL file into a newly spawned Internet Explorer process.
Remsec can perform DLL injection.

techniques.name: Portable Executable Injection
techniques.summary: Adversaries may inject portable executables (PE) into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

procedures.text: Brute Ratel C4 has injected Latrodectus into the Explorer.exe process on comrpomised hosts.
InvisiMole can inject its backdoor as a portable executable into a target process.
Havoc has itself injected into `C:\\Windows\\System32\\Werfault.exe` on targeted systems.
Carbanak downloads an executable and injects it directly into a new process.

techniques.name: Thread Execution Hijacking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into hijacked processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

procedures.text: Pikabot can create a suspended instance of a legitimate process (e.g., ctfmon.exe), allocate memory within the suspended process corresponding to Pikabot's core module, then redirect execution flow via `SetContextThread` API so that when...
Waterbear can use thread injection to inject shellcode into the process of security software.
Gazer performs thread execution hijacking to inject its orchestrator into a running thread from a remote process.
Trojan.Karagany can inject a suspended thread of its own process into a new process and initiate via the ResumeThread API.

techniques.name: Asynchronous Procedure Call
techniques.summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via the asynchronous procedure call (APC) queue in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

procedures.text: TURNEDUP is capable of injecting code into the APC queue of a created Rundll32 process as part of an "Early Bird injection."
HeartCrypt has the ability to use `NtQueueApcThread` as an alternate method for process injection.
Pillowmint has used the NtQueueApcThread syscall to inject code into svchost.exe.
InvisiMole can inject its code into a trusted process via the APC queue.

techniques.name: Thread Local Storage
techniques.summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via thread local storage (TLS) callbacks in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

procedures.text: CANONSTAGER uses the Thread Local Storage (TLS) array data structure to store function addresses resolved by its custom API hashing algorithm. The function addresses are later called throughout the binary from offsets into the TLS array.
Ursnif has injected code into target processes via thread local storage callbacks.

techniques.name: Ptrace System Calls
techniques.summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via ptrace (process trace) system calls in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

procedures.text: PACEMAKER can use PTRACE to attach to a targeted process to read process memory.

techniques.name: Proc Memory
techniques.summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via the /proc filesystem in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Extra Window Memory Injection
techniques.summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into process via Extra Window Memory (EWM) in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

procedures.text: Epic has overwritten the function pointer in the extra window memory of Explorer's Shell_TrayWnd in order to execute malicious code in the context of the explorer.exe process.

Power Loader overwrites Explorer’s Shell_TrayWnd extra window memory to redirect execution to a NTDLL function that is abused to assemble and execute a return-oriented programming (ROP) chain and create a malicious thread within Explorer...

techniques.name: Process Hollowing
techniques.summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into suspended and hollowed processes in order to evade process-based defenses.

procedures.text: Vidar has used process hollowing to inject itself into an AppLaunch.exe process.
Gorgon Group malware can use process hollowing to inject one of its trojans into another process.
IcedID can inject a Cobalt Strike beacon into cmd.exe via process hallowing.
XLoader uses process hollowing by injecting itself into the `explorer.exe` process and other files ithin the Windows `SysWOW64` directory.

techniques.name: Process Doppelgänging
techniques.summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into process via process doppelgänging in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

procedures.text: SynAck abuses NTFS transactions to launch and conceal malicious processes.
Bazar can inject into a target process using process doppelgänging.
Leafminer has used Process Doppelgänging to evade security software while deploying tools on compromised systems.

techniques.name: VDSO Hijacking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via VDSO hijacking in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: ListPlanting
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse list-view controls to inject malicious code into hijacked processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

procedures.text: InvisiMole has used ListPlanting to inject code into a trusted process.

techniques.name: Input Capture
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use methods of capturing user input to obtain credentials or collect information.

procedures.text: InvisibleFerret has collected mouse and keyboard events using “pyWinhook”.
APT42 has used credential harvesting websites.
Storm-1811 has used a PowerShell script to capture user credentials after prompting a user to authenticate to run a malicious script masquerading as a legitimate update item.
metaMain can log mouse events.

techniques.name: Keylogging
techniques.summary: Adversaries may log user keystrokes to intercept credentials as the user types them.

procedures.text: Magic Hound malware is capable of keylogging.
Derusbi is capable of logging keystrokes.
PowerLess can use a module to log keystrokes.
Peppy can log keystrokes on compromised hosts.

techniques.name: GUI Input Capture
techniques.summary: Adversaries may mimic common operating system GUI components to prompt users for credentials with a seemingly legitimate prompt.

procedures.text: Proton prompts users for their credentials.
APT38 has leveraged a fictitious native macOS password dialog prompt to entice victims to enter credentials.
LP-Notes has displayed a fake Windows Security dialog box to prompt for Windows credentials.
iKitten prompts the user for their credentials.

techniques.name: Web Portal Capture
techniques.summary: Adversaries may install code on externally facing portals, such as a VPN login page, to capture and transmit credentials of users who attempt to log into the service.

procedures.text: Kimsuky has collected credentials from a fake Google account login page.
Winter Vivern registered and hosted domains to allow for creation of web pages mimicking legitimate government email logon sites to collect logon information.
WARPWIRE can capture credentials submitted during the web logon process in order to access layer seven applications such as RDP.
The IceApple OWA credential logger can monitor for OWA authentication requests and log the credentials.

techniques.name: Credential API Hooking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may hook into Windows application programming interface (API) functions and Linux system functions to collect user credentials.

procedures.text: Zeus Panda hooks processes by leveraging its own IAT hooked functions.
VersaMem hooked and overrided Versa's built-in authentication method, `setUserPassword`, to intercept plaintext credentials when submitted to the server.
Carberp has hooked several Windows API functions to steal credentials.
FinFisher hooks processes by modifying IAT pointers to CreateWindowEx.

techniques.name: Process Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to get information about running processes on a system. Information obtained could be used to gain an understanding of common software/applications running on systems within the network.

procedures.text: Epic uses the tasklist /v command to obtain a list of processes.
SPAWNCHIMERA has searched for running processes to include web or dsmdm.
WarzoneRAT can obtain a list of processes on a compromised host.
FELIXROOT collects a list of running processes.

techniques.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands, scripts, or binaries.

procedures.text: Fox Kitten has used a Perl reverse shell to communicate with C2.
Stealth Falcon malware uses WMI to script data collection and command execution on the victim.
Winter Vivern used XLM 4.0 macros for initial code execution for malicious document files.
FIN7 used SQL scripts to help perform tasks on the victim's machine.

techniques.name: PowerShell
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution. PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting environment included in the Windows operating system.

procedures.text: WIRTE has used PowerShell for script execution.
RansomHub can use PowerShell to delete volume shadow copies.
APT42 has downloaded and executed PowerShell payloads.
APT5 has used PowerShell to accomplish tasks within targeted environments.

techniques.name: AppleScript
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse AppleScript for execution. AppleScript is a macOS scripting language designed to control applications and parts of the OS via inter-application messages called AppleEvents.

procedures.text: APT38 has sent Mac users.scpt files to trigger malicious downloads. APT38 has targeted macOS uses with native script stagers leading to malicious paylaods. APT38 has also used an AppleScript-based credential harvesting component.
Dok uses AppleScript to create a login item for persistence.
ThiefQuest uses AppleScript's osascript -e command to launch ThiefQuest's persistence via Launch Agent and Launch Daemon.
GlassWorm has utilized AppleScript to include `set keychainPassword to do shell script` to execute shell command that retrieves passwords from the macOS keychain.

techniques.name: Windows Command Shell
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse the Windows command shell for execution. The Windows command shell (cmd) is the primary command prompt on Windows systems.

procedures.text: SeaDuke is capable of executing commands.
Lazarus Group malware uses cmd.exe to execute commands on a compromised host. A Destover-like variant used by Lazarus Group uses a batch file mechanism to delete its binaries from the system.
InnaputRAT launches a shell to execute commands on the victim’s machine.
Daserf can execute shell commands.

techniques.name: Unix Shell
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse Unix shell commands and scripts for execution. Unix shells are the primary command prompt on Linux, macOS, and ESXi systems, though many variations of the Unix shell exist (e.g.

procedures.text: BOLDMOVE is capable of spawning a remote command shell.
CASTLETAP has the ability to spawn BusyBox command shell in victim environments.
Aquatic Panda used malicious shell scripts in Linux environments following access via SSH to install Linux versions of Winnti malware.
Ebury can use the commands `Xcsh` or `Xcls` to open a shell with Ebury level permissions and `Xxsh` to open a shell with root level.

techniques.name: Visual Basic
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse Visual Basic (VB) for execution.

procedures.text: Lokibot has used VBS scripts and XLS macros for execution.
Patchwork used Visual Basic Scripts (VBS) on victim machines.
Grandoreiro can use VBScript to execute malicious code.
BackConfig has used VBS to install its downloader component and malicious documents with VBA macro code.

techniques.name: Python
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse Python commands and scripts for execution. Python is a very popular scripting/programming language, with capabilities to perform many functions.

procedures.text: IronNetInjector can use IronPython scripts to load payloads with the help of a .NET injector.
DropBook is a Python-based backdoor compiled with PyInstaller.
VIRTUALPIE is a Python-based backdoor malware.
PUNCHBUGGY has used python scripts.

techniques.name: JavaScript
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse various implementations of JavaScript for execution.

procedures.text: TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has infected victims through malicious pre and post-install scripts within the package.json file.
AppleSeed has the ability to use JavaScript to execute PowerShell.
The Cobalt Strike System Profiler can use JavaScript to perform reconnaissance actions.
Metamorfo includes payloads written in JavaScript.

techniques.name: Network Device CLI
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse scripting or built-in command line interpreters (CLI) on network devices to execute malicious command and payloads.

procedures.text: DRYHOOK has the ability to interact with Ivanti Connect Secure environments and to modify system components.

Salt Typhoon has executed commands on network devices using the native command line interface. Salt Typhoon has leveraged Tcl scripts on Cisco IOS devices to include `TCLprox.tcl` and `map.tcl` when `tclsh` was available. Salt Typhoon al...
Line Dancer can execute native commands in networking device command line interfaces.
PHASEJAM has leveraged native commands associated with the compromised network appliance to execute code.

techniques.name: Cloud API
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse cloud APIs to execute malicious commands.

procedures.text: Storm-0501 has leveraged Cloud CLI to execute commands and exfiltrate data from compromised environments.
TruffleHog has leveraged Cloud CLI in order to enumerate and gather credentials.
ShinyHunters has used the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI) for operations to include a variety of API calls, such as `ListBuckets`, `CreateBucket` and `DeleteBucket`.
Pacu leverages the AWS CLI for its operations.

techniques.name: AutoHotKey & AutoIT
techniques.summary: Adversaries may execute commands and perform malicious tasks using AutoIT and AutoHotKey automation scripts. AutoIT and AutoHotkey (AHK) are scripting languages that enable users to automate Windows tasks.

procedures.text: Lumma Stealer has utilized AutoIt malware scripts and AutoIt executables.
Melcoz has been distributed through an AutoIt loader script.
XLoader can use an AutoIT script to decrypt a payload file, load it into victim memory, then execute it on the victim machine.
OutSteel was developed using the AutoIT scripting language.

techniques.name: Lua
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse Lua commands and scripts for execution. Lua is a cross-platform scripting and programming language primarily designed for embedded use in applications.

procedures.text: EvilBunny has used Lua scripts to execute payloads.
Remsec can use modules written in Lua for execution.
RedLine Stealer malware has leveraged Lua bytecode to perform malicious behavior.
Line Runner utilizes Lua scripts for command execution.

techniques.name: Hypervisor CLI
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse hypervisor command line interpreters (CLIs) to execute malicious commands.

procedures.text: UNC3886 has used the esxcli command line utility to modify firewall rules, install malware, and for artifact removal.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has utilized `esxcli` to execute commands on compromised ESXi systems and VMs.
Cheerscrypt has leveraged `esxcli` in order to terminate running virtual machines.
Royal ransomware uses `esxcli` to gather a list of running VMs and terminate them.

techniques.name: Container CLI/API
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse built-in CLI tools or API calls to execute malicious commands in containerized environments. The Docker CLI is used for managing containers via an exposed API point from the `dockerd` daemon.

procedures.text: TeamTNT targeted misconfigured containers and used container CLI tools.
TeamPCP has queried the Kubernetes API for local service account tokens and has used `kubectl` for lateral movement.
Mini Shai-Hulud has utilized the Docker command-line tool to gather details of the victim environment and collect credentials.
Salt Typhoon has leveraged Cisco Guest Shell to interact with a Linux Container on network devices.

techniques.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to elevate privileges.

procedures.text: Threat Group-3390 has used CVE-2014-6324 and CVE-2017-0213 to escalate privileges.

Embargo has leveraged MS4Killer to deliver a vulnerable driver to the victim device, sometimes referred to as Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD). Embargo has utilized the vulnerable driver probmon.sys version 3.0.0.4 which had a re...
Remsec has a plugin to drop and execute vulnerable Outpost Sandbox or avast! Virtualization drivers in order to gain kernel mode privileges.
The Gentlemen has assisted affiliates with gaining privilege escalation through the use of BYOVD.

techniques.name: Permission Groups Discovery
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to discover group and permission settings.

procedures.text: APT41 used net group commands to enumerate various Windows user groups and permissions.
IcedID has the ability to identify Workgroup membership.
Carbon uses the net group command.
TrickBot can identify the groups the user on a compromised host belongs to.

techniques.name: Local Groups
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to find local system groups and permission settings. The knowledge of local system permission groups can help adversaries determine which groups exist and which users belong to a particular group.

procedures.text: Turla has used net localgroup and net localgroup Administrators to enumerate group information, including members of the local administrators group.
JPIN can obtain the permissions of the victim user.
Sys10 collects the group name of the logged-in user and sends it to the C2.
BloodHound can collect information about local groups and members.

techniques.name: Domain Groups
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to find domain-level groups and permission settings. The knowledge of domain-level permission groups can help adversaries determine which groups exist and which users belong to a particular group.

procedures.text: Kwampirs collects a list of domain groups with the command net localgroup /domain .
LAPSUS$ has used the AD Explorer tool to enumerate groups on a victim's network.
Commands such as net group /domain can be used in Net to gather information about and manipulate groups.
BloodHound can collect information about domain groups and members.

techniques.name: Cloud Groups
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to find cloud groups and permission settings.

procedures.text: ROADTools can enumerate Azure AD groups.
AADInternals can enumerate Azure AD groups.
Pacu can enumerate IAM permissions.
ShinyHunters has executed API calls to enumerate permissions for compromised AWS accounts.

techniques.name: Indicator Removal
techniques.summary: Adversaries may selectively delete or modify artifacts generated to reduce indications of their presence and blend in with legitimate activity.

procedures.text: IPsec Helper can delete various registry keys related to its execution and use.
Donut can erase file references to payloads in-memory after being reflectively loaded and executed.
SDBbot has the ability to clean up and remove data structures from a compromised host.
BPFDoor clears the file location `/proc/ /environ` removing all environment variables for the process.

techniques.name: Clear Command History
techniques.summary: In addition to clearing system logs, an adversary may clear the command history of a compromised account to conceal the actions undertaken during an intrusion.

procedures.text: The Gentlemen Ransomware has deleted PowerShell command history for all users by targeting the command history file located in `C:/Users/*/AppData/Roaming/Microsoft/Windows/PowerShell/PSReadline/ConsoleHost_History.txt`.
Aquatic Panda cleared command history in Linux environments to remove traces of activity after operations.
J-magic can overwrite previously executed command line arguments.
APT38 has executed scripts to delete the PowerShell command history file.

techniques.name: File Deletion
techniques.summary: Adversaries may delete files left behind by the actions of their intrusion activity.

procedures.text: TDTESS creates then deletes log files during installation of itself as a service.
LODEINFO can delete files to remove traces of activity from victim systems.
LightNeuron has a function to delete files.
ROADSWEEP can use embedded scripts to remove itself from the infected host.

techniques.name: Network Share Connection Removal
techniques.summary: Adversaries may remove share connections that are no longer useful in order to clean up traces of their operation. Windows shared drive and SMB/Windows Admin Shares connections can be removed when no longer needed.

procedures.text: The net use \\system\share /delete command can be used in Net to remove an established connection to a network share.
RobbinHood disconnects all network shares from the computer with the command net use * /DELETE /Y .
DUSTTRAP can remove network shares from infected systems.
InvisiMole can disconnect previously connected remote drives.

techniques.name: Timestomp
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify file time attributes to hide new files or changes to existing files.

procedures.text: TAINTEDSCRIBE can change the timestamp of specified filenames.
APT28 has performed timestomping on victim files.
Cyclops Blink has the ability to use the Linux API function `utime` to change the timestamps of modified firmware update images.
APT5 has modified file timestamps.

techniques.name: Clear Network Connection History and Configurations
techniques.summary: Adversaries may clear or remove evidence of malicious network connections in order to clean up traces of their operations.

procedures.text: Salt Typhoon has reverted or modified network configuration files to remove traces of activity.

NIMBUS MANTICORE has cleared RDP connection history registry keys to include `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Terminal Server Client\Default` and ` HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Terminal Server Client\Servers`.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has removed RDP Logs by leveraging the command `del /f /q %SystemRoot%\System32\LogFiles\RDP\\.`.
UNC3886 has cleared specific events that contained the threat actor’s IP address from multiple log sources.

techniques.name: Clear Mailbox Data
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify mail and mail application data to remove evidence of their activity. Email applications allow users and other programs to export and delete mailbox data via command line tools or use of APIs.

procedures.text: LunarMail can set the `PR_DELETE_AFTER_SUBMIT` flag to delete messages sent for data exfiltration.
APT42 has deleted login notification emails and has cleared the Sent folder to cover their tracks.
Goopy has the ability to delete emails used for C2 once the content has been copied.
