Mustang Panda leveraged a captive portal hijack that redirected the victim to a webpage that prompted the victim to download a malicious payload.

Kali365 has created obfuscated phishing landing pages that act as an adversary in the middle infrastructure that intercepts communications between the victim host and legitimate services to steal credentials and user sessions.

evilginx2 has the ability to act as an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) relay between a legitimate website and a phished user to capture all transmitted data including usernames, passwords, authentication tokens, and session cookies and to...

techniques.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
techniques.summary: By responding to LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS network traffic, adversaries may spoof an authoritative source for name resolution to force communication with an adversary controlled system.

procedures.text: Impacket modules like ntlmrelayx and smbrelayx can be used in conjunction with Network Sniffing and Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay to gather NetNTLM credentials for Brute Force or relay attacks that can gain code execution.
Empire can use Inveigh to conduct name service poisoning for credential theft and associated relay attacks.
PoshC2 can use Inveigh to conduct name service poisoning for credential theft and associated relay attacks.
Lazarus Group executed Responder using the command [Responder file path] -i [IP address] -rPv on a compromised host to harvest credentials and move laterally.

techniques.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
techniques.summary: Adversaries may poison Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) caches to position themselves between the communication of two or more networked devices.

procedures.text: Cleaver has used custom tools to facilitate ARP cache poisoning.
LuminousMoth has used ARP spoofing to redirect a compromised machine to an actor-controlled website.

techniques.name: DHCP Spoofing
techniques.summary: Adversaries may redirect network traffic to adversary-owned systems by spoofing Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) traffic and acting as a malicious DHCP server on the victim network.

techniques.name: Evil Twin
techniques.summary: Adversaries may host seemingly genuine Wi-Fi access points to deceive users into connecting to malicious networks as a way of supporting follow-on behaviors such as Network Sniffing, Transmitted Data Manipulation, or...

procedures.text: APT28 has used a Wi-Fi Pineapple to set up Evil Twin Wi-Fi Poisoning for the purposes of capturing victim credentials or planting espionage-oriented malware.

techniques.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to subvert Kerberos authentication by stealing or forging Kerberos tickets to enable Pass the Ticket.

procedures.text: Akira have used scripts to dump Kerberos authentication credentials.

techniques.name: Golden Ticket
techniques.summary: Adversaries who have the KRBTGT account password hash may forge Kerberos ticket-granting tickets (TGT), also known as a golden ticket.

procedures.text: Ke3chang has used Mimikatz to generate Kerberos golden tickets.
Empire can leverage its implementation of Mimikatz to obtain and use golden tickets.
Mimikatz's kerberos module can create golden tickets.
Sliver incorporates the Rubeus framework to allow for Kerberos ticket manipulation, specifically for forging Kerberos Golden Tickets.

techniques.name: Silver Ticket
techniques.summary: Adversaries who have the password hash of a target service account (e.g. SharePoint, MSSQL) may forge Kerberos ticket granting service (TGS) tickets, also known as silver tickets.

procedures.text: Rubeus can create silver tickets.
AADInternals can be used to forge Kerberos tickets using the password hash of the AZUREADSSOACC account.
Mimikatz's kerberos module can create silver tickets.
Empire can leverage its implementation of Mimikatz to obtain and use silver tickets.

techniques.name: Kerberoasting
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse a valid Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) or sniff network traffic to obtain a ticket-granting service (TGS) ticket that may be vulnerable to Brute Force.

procedures.text: Rubeus can use the `KerberosRequestorSecurityToken.GetRequest` method to request kerberoastable service tickets.
Impacket modules like GetUserSPNs can be used to get Service Principal Names (SPNs) for user accounts. The output is formatted to be compatible with cracking tools like John the Ripper and Hashcat.
Empire uses PowerSploit's Invoke-Kerberoast to request service tickets and return crackable ticket hashes.
Wizard Spider has used Rubeus, MimiKatz Kerberos module, and the Invoke-Kerberoast cmdlet to steal AES hashes.

techniques.name: AS-REP Roasting
techniques.summary: Adversaries may reveal credentials of accounts that have disabled Kerberos preauthentication by Password Cracking Kerberos messages.

procedures.text: Rubeus can reveal the credentials of accounts that have Kerberos pre-authentication disabled through AS-REP roasting.

techniques.name: Ccache Files
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to steal Kerberos tickets stored in credential cache files (or ccache). These files are used for short term storage of a user's active session credentials.

procedures.text: Impacket tools – such as getST.py or ticketer.py – can be used to steal or forge Kerberos tickets using ccache files given a password, hash, aesKey, or TGT.

techniques.name: Inter-Process Communication
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms for local code or command execution. IPC is typically used by processes to share data, communicate with each other, or synchronize execution.

procedures.text: The Havoc SMB demon can use named pipes for communication through a parent demon.
StealBit can use interprocess communication (IPC) to enable the designation of multiple files for exfiltration in a scalable manner.
Raspberry Robin contains an embedded custom Tor network client that communicates with the primary payload via shared process memory.
MiniBrowse has sent JSON files to a named pipe.

techniques.name: Component Object Model
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use the Windows Component Object Model (COM) for local code execution.

procedures.text: POWERSTATS can use DCOM (targeting the 127.0.0.1 loopback address) to execute additional payloads on compromised hosts.
TrickBot used COM to setup scheduled task for persistence.
CLAIMLOADER has leveraged Component Object Model (COM) objects to create a scheduled task using `ITaskService` interface.

Kimsuky has leveraged Component Object Model (COM) to create scheduled tasks to include using naming conventions that mimic legitimate applications. Kimsuky has leveraged obfuscation VBScript to form a string in `WScript.Shell` which has...

techniques.name: Dynamic Data Exchange
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use Windows Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) to execute arbitrary commands. DDE is a client-server protocol for one-time and/or continuous inter-process communication (IPC) between applications.

procedures.text: Ramsay has been delivered using OLE objects in malicious documents.
HAWKBALL has used an OLE object that uses Equation Editor to drop the embedded shellcode.
Cobalt Group has sent malicious Word OLE compound documents to victims.
FIN7 spear phishing campaigns have included malicious Word documents with DDE execution.

techniques.name: XPC Services
techniques.summary: Adversaries can provide malicious content to an XPC service daemon for local code execution.

techniques.name: Archive Collected Data
techniques.summary: An adversary may compress and/or encrypt data that is collected prior to exfiltration. Compressing the data can help to obfuscate the collected data and minimize the amount of data sent over the network.

procedures.text: Dragonfly has compressed data into .zip files prior to exfiltration.
Chrommme can encrypt and store on disk collected data before exfiltration.
Patchwork encrypted the collected files' path with AES and then encoded them with base64.
Exaramel for Windows automatically encrypts files before sending them to the C2 server.

techniques.name: Archive via Utility
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use utilities to compress and/or encrypt collected data prior to exfiltration.

procedures.text: Crutch has used the WinRAR utility to compress and encrypt stolen files.
Okrum was seen using a RAR archiver tool to compress/decompress data.
HAFNIUM has used 7-Zip and WinRAR to compress stolen files for exfiltration.
certutil may be used to Base64 encode collected data.

techniques.name: Archive via Library
techniques.summary: An adversary may compress or encrypt data that is collected prior to exfiltration using 3rd party libraries. Many libraries exist that can archive data, including Python rarfile , libzip , and zlib .

procedures.text: TajMahal has the ability to use the open source libraries XZip/Xunzip and zlib to compress files.
ShinyHunters has used the following command to compress collected data: ` pv -s "$(du -sb exfil | awk '{print $1}')" | zstd -3 -T0 -o exfil.tar.zst `.
LunarWeb can zlib-compress data prior to exfiltration.
The ZLib backdoor compresses communications using the standard Zlib compression library.

techniques.name: Archive via Custom Method
techniques.summary: An adversary may compress or encrypt data that is collected prior to exfiltration using a custom method.

procedures.text: Attor encrypts collected data with a custom implementation of Blowfish and RSA ciphers.
BLUELIGHT has encoded data into a binary blob using XOR.
FIN6 has encoded data gathered from the victim with a simple substitution cipher and single-byte XOR using the 0xAA key, and Base64 with character permutation.
Modules can be pushed to and executed by Duqu that copy data to a staging area, compress it, and XOR encrypt it.

techniques.name: Disk Wipe
techniques.summary: Adversaries may wipe or corrupt raw disk data on specific systems or in large numbers in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources.

techniques.name: Disk Content Wipe
techniques.summary: Adversaries may erase the contents of storage devices on specific systems or in large numbers in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources.

procedures.text: VOID MANTICORE has utilized a disk wiping utility to facilitate destructive actions on victim servers. VOID MANTICORE has also utilized legitimate remote disk wiping commands.
cipher.exe can be used to overwrite deleted data in specified folders.
DEADWOOD deletes files following overwriting them with random data.
AcidRain iterates over device file identifiers on the target, opens the device file, and either overwrites the file or calls various IOCTLS commands to erase it.

techniques.name: Disk Structure Wipe
techniques.summary: Adversaries may corrupt or wipe the disk data structures on a hard drive necessary to boot a system; targeting specific critical systems or in large numbers in a network to interrupt availability to system and network...

procedures.text: Shamoon has been seen overwriting features of disk structure such as the MBR.
Diskpart can be used to delete a partition or a volume. Diskpart can also be used to remove all partitions or volume formatting from the selected disk.
HermeticWiper has the ability to corrupt disk partitions, damage the Master Boot Record (MBR), and overwrite the Master File Table (MFT) of all available physical drives.
RawDisk was used in Shamoon to help overwrite components of disk structure like the MBR and disk partitions.

techniques.name: Remote Service Session Hijacking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may take control of preexisting sessions with remote services to move laterally in an environment.

techniques.name: SSH Hijacking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may hijack a legitimate user's SSH session to move laterally within an environment. Secure Shell (SSH) is a standard means of remote access on Linux and macOS systems.

procedures.text: MEDUSA can be configured to capture SSH credentials via SSH hijacking.

techniques.name: RDP Hijacking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may hijack a legitimate user’s remote desktop session to move laterally within an environment. Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems.

procedures.text: NIMBUS MANTICORE has conducted RDP session hijacking to gain access to victim devices.
WannaCry enumerates current remote desktop sessions and tries to execute the malware on each session.
Axiom has targeted victims with remote administration tools including RDP.

techniques.name: Hide Artifacts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to hide artifacts associated with their behaviors to evade detection.

procedures.text: OSX/Shlayer has used the mktemp utility to make random and unique filenames for payloads, such as export tmpDir="$(mktemp -d /tmp/XXXXXXXXXXXX)" or mktemp -t Installer .
Bundlore uses the mktemp utility to make unique file and directory names for payloads, such as TMP_DIR=`mktemp -d -t x .
WarzoneRAT can masquerade the Process Environment Block on a compromised host to hide its attempts to elevate privileges through `IFileOperation`.
DarkTortilla has used `%HiddenReg%` and `%HiddenKey%` as part of its persistence via the Windows registry.

techniques.name: Hidden Files and Directories
techniques.summary: Adversaries may set files and directories to be hidden to evade detection mechanisms.

procedures.text: QakBot has placed its payload in hidden subdirectories.
XCSSET uses a hidden folder named .xcassets and .git to embed itself in Xcode.
APT28 has saved files with hidden file attributes.
RedCurl added the “hidden” file attribute to original files, manipulating victims to click on malicious LNK files.

techniques.name: Hidden Users
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use hidden users to hide the presence of user accounts they create or modify.

procedures.text: Dragonfly has modified the Registry to hide created user accounts.
SMOKEDHAM has modified the Registry to hide created user accounts from the Windows logon screen.
Kimsuky has run reg add ‘HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\SpecialAccounts\UserList’ /v to hide a newly created user.

techniques.name: Hidden Window
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use hidden windows to conceal malicious activity from the plain sight of users. In some cases, windows that would typically be displayed when an application carries out an operation can be hidden.

procedures.text: Astaroth loads its module with the XSL script parameter vShow set to zero, which opens the application with a hidden window.
QuietSieve has the ability to execute payloads in a hidden window.
StrongPity has the ability to hide the console window for its document search module from the user.
LockBit 2.0 can execute command line arguments in a hidden window.

techniques.name: NTFS File Attributes
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use NTFS file attributes to hide their malicious data in order to evade detection.

procedures.text: The Regin malware platform uses Extended Attributes to store encrypted executables.
APT32 used NTFS alternate data streams to hide their payloads.
Valak has the ability save and execute files as alternate data streams (ADS).
LoJax has loaded an embedded NTFS DXE driver to be able to access and write to NTFS partitions.

techniques.name: Hidden File System
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use a hidden file system to conceal malicious activity from users and security tools. File systems provide a structure to store and access data from physical storage.

procedures.text: Equation has used an encrypted virtual file system stored in the Windows Registry.
ComRAT has used a portable FAT16 partition image placed in %TEMP% as a hidden file system.
Regin has used a hidden file system to store some of its components.
BOOTRASH has used unallocated disk space between partitions for a hidden file system that stores components of the Nemesis bootkit.

techniques.name: Run Virtual Instance
techniques.summary: Adversaries may carry out malicious operations using a virtual instance to avoid detection. A wide variety of virtualization technologies exist that allow for the emulation of a computer or computing environment.

procedures.text: Maze operators have used VirtualBox and a Windows 7 virtual machine to run the ransomware; the virtual machine's configuration file mapped the shared network drives of the target company, presumably so Maze can encrypt files on the share...

Ragnar Locker has used VirtualBox and a stripped Windows XP virtual machine to run itself. The use of a shared folder specified in the configuration enables Ragnar Locker to encrypt files on the host operating system, including files on...
LoudMiner has used QEMU and VirtualBox to run a Tiny Core Linux virtual machine, which runs XMRig and makes connections to the C2 server for updates.

techniques.name: VBA Stomping
techniques.summary: Adversaries may hide malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) payloads embedded within MS Office documents by replacing the VBA source code with benign data.

techniques.name: Email Hiding Rules
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use email rules to hide inbound emails in a compromised user's mailbox.

procedures.text: Scattered Spider creates inbound rules on the compromised email accounts of security personnel to automatically delete emails from vendor security products.

FIN4 has created rules in victims' Microsoft Outlook accounts to automatically delete emails containing words such as “hacked," "phish," and “malware" in a likely attempt to prevent organizations from communicating about their activities.
Kali365 has the ability to modify email rules to delete email based notifications prior to the victim seeing them.

techniques.name: Resource Forking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse resource forks to hide malicious code or executables to evade detection and bypass security applications.

procedures.text: Keydnap uses a resource fork to present a macOS JPEG or text file icon rather than the executable's icon assigned by the operating system.
OSX/Shlayer has used a resource fork to hide a compressed binary file of itself from the terminal, Finder, and potentially evade traditional scanners.

techniques.name: Process Argument Spoofing
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to hide process command-line arguments by overwriting process memory.

procedures.text: Cobalt Strike can use spoof arguments in spawned processes that execute beacon commands.
SombRAT has the ability to modify its process memory to hide process command-line arguments.

techniques.name: Ignore Process Interrupts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may evade defensive mechanisms by executing commands that hide from process interrupt signals. Many operating systems use signals to deliver messages to control process behavior.

procedures.text: APT38 has used remote access tools that run AppleScript using ` nohup osascript` to ignore hangup signals.
The GoldMax Linux variant has been executed with the `nohup` command to ignore hangup signals and continue to run if the terminal session was terminated.
BOLDMOVE calls the signal function to ignore the signals SIGCHLD, SIGHIP, and SIGPIPE prior to starting primary logic.
UNC3886 modified the startup file `/etc/init.d/localnet` to execute the line `nohup /bin/support &` so the script would run when the system was rebooted.

techniques.name: File/Path Exclusions
techniques.summary: Adversaries may attempt to hide their file-based artifacts by writing them to specific folders or file names excluded from antivirus (AV) scanning and other defensive capabilities.

procedures.text: Turla has placed LunarWeb install files into directories that are excluded from scanning.

The Gentlemen Ransomware has modified anti-virus settings to add its own executable to the exclusion list of the endpoint detection solution using the PowerShell command `Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess -force`.
APT38 has added Microsoft Defender exclusions to include `C:\Windows\System32` to suppress detection of dropped tooling.

techniques.name: Bind Mounts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse bind mounts on file structures to hide their activity and artifacts from native utilities.

techniques.name: Extended Attributes
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse extended attributes (xattrs) on macOS and Linux to hide their malicious data in order to evade detection.

techniques.name: Data Manipulation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may insert, delete, or manipulate data in order to influence external outcomes or hide activity, thus threatening the integrity of the data.

procedures.text: FIN13 has injected fraudulent transactions into compromised networks that mimic legitimate behavior to siphon off incremental amounts of money.
PHASEJAM has blocked legitimate upgrades of Ivanti Connect Secure systems and falsely indicates a successful upgrade while operating on an older version.

techniques.name: Stored Data Manipulation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may insert, delete, or manipulate data at rest in order to influence external outcomes or hide activity, thus threatening the integrity of the data.

procedures.text: SUNSPOT created a copy of the SolarWinds Orion software source file with a .bk extension to backup the original content, wrote SUNBURST using the same filename but with a .tmp extension, and then moved SUNBURST using MoveFileEx to the or...

APT38 has used DYEPACK to create, delete, and alter records in databases used for SWIFT transactions.

techniques.name: Transmitted Data Manipulation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may alter data en route to storage or other systems in order to manipulate external outcomes or hide activity, thus threatening the integrity of the data.

procedures.text: Melcoz can monitor the clipboard for cryptocurrency addresses and change the intended address to one controlled by the adversary.
APT38 has used DYEPACK to manipulate SWIFT messages en route to a printer.
GlassWorm can intercept and modify transaction details associated with hardware wallet applications before signing.
LightNeuron is capable of modifying email content, headers, and attachments during transit.

techniques.name: Runtime Data Manipulation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify systems in order to manipulate the data as it is accessed and displayed to an end user, thus threatening the integrity of the data.

procedures.text: APT38 has used DYEPACK.FOX to manipulate PDF data as it is accessed to remove traces of fraudulent SWIFT transactions from the data displayed to the end user.

techniques.name: Phishing
techniques.summary: Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering.

procedures.text: Hikit has been spread through spear phishing.
Kimsuky has used spearphishing to gain initial access and intelligence.
INC Ransomware campaigns have used spearphishing emails for initial access.
VOID MANTICORE has emailed victims threatening messages. VOID MANTICORE has used phishing as an initial access vector.

techniques.name: Spearphishing Attachment
techniques.summary: Adversaries may send spearphishing emails with a malicious attachment in an attempt to gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing attachment is a specific variant of spearphishing.

procedures.text: Cobalt Group has sent spearphishing emails with various attachment types to corporate and personal email accounts of victim organizations. Attachment types have included .rtf, .doc, .xls, archives containing LNK files, and password prote...
KOCTOPUS has been distributed via spearphishing emails with malicious attachments.
Lokibot is delivered via a malicious XLS attachment contained within a spearhpishing email.
Lazarus Group has targeted victims with spearphishing emails containing malicious Microsoft Word documents.

techniques.name: Spearphishing Link
techniques.summary: Adversaries may send spearphishing emails with a malicious link in an attempt to gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing with a link is a specific variant of spearphishing.

procedures.text: BlackTech has used spearphishing e-mails with links to cloud services to deliver malware.
Kerrdown has been distributed via e-mails containing a malicious link.
MuddyWater has sent targeted spearphishing e-mails with malicious links.
LuminousMoth has sent spearphishing emails containing a malicious Dropbox download link.

techniques.name: Spearphishing via Service
techniques.summary: Adversaries may send spearphishing messages via third-party services in an attempt to gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing via service is a specific variant of spearphishing.

procedures.text: CURIUM has used social media to deliver malicious files to victims.
Windshift has used fake personas on social media to engage and target victims.
Ajax Security Team has used various social media channels to spearphish victims.
EXOTIC LILY has used the e-mail notification features of legitimate file sharing services for spearphishing.

techniques.name: Spearphishing Voice
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use voice communications to ultimately gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing voice is a specific variant of spearphishing.

procedures.text: Storm-1811 has initiated voice calls with victims posing as IT support to prompt users to download and execute scripts and other tools for initial access.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Web Service
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service to exfiltrate data rather than their primary command and control channel.

procedures.text: Magic Hound has used the Telegram API `sendMessage` to relay data on compromised devices.
Contagious Interview has leveraged Telegram API to exfiltrate stolen data.
OilCheck can upload documents from compromised hosts to a shared Microsoft Office 365 Outlook email account for exfiltration.
APT28 can exfiltrate data over Google Drive.

techniques.name: Exfiltration to Code Repository
techniques.summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to a code repository rather than over their primary command and control channel. Code repositories are often accessible via an API (ex: https://api.github.com).

procedures.text: Mini Shai-Hulud has exfiltrated data through the use of the victim’s own GitHub repository by creating a new public repository using a unique naming convention from a curated list of key words or themes.
Empire can use GitHub for data exfiltration.

Shai-Hulud has created a repository named `Shai-Hulud` under the compromised account that commits a JSON dump that contains system information, environment variables and collected secrets. Shai-Hulud has also posted stolen credentials to...
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can create a repository in the victim's GitHub account using the victim's own GITHUB_TOKEN to upload stolen credentials.

techniques.name: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
techniques.summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to a cloud storage service rather than over their primary command and control channel.

procedures.text: Leviathan has used an uploader known as LUNCHMONEY that can exfiltrate files to Dropbox.
Akira will exfiltrate victim data using applications such as Rclone.
LuminousMoth has exfiltrated data to Google Drive.
Tsundere Botnet’s variant DinDoor has used Rclone to access a Wasabi server.

techniques.name: Exfiltration to Text Storage Sites
techniques.summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to text storage sites instead of their primary command and control channel.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Webhook
techniques.summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to a webhook endpoint rather than over their primary command and control channel.

procedures.text: Shai-Hulud has exfiltrated repository secrets to `webhook[.]site`.

techniques.name: Dynamic Resolution
techniques.summary: Adversaries may dynamically establish connections to command and control infrastructure to evade common detections and remediations.

procedures.text: Tomiris has connected to a signalization server that provides a URL and port, and then Tomiris sends a GET request to that URL to establish C2.
RedEcho used dynamic DNS domains associated with malicious infrastructure.
Gelsemium can use dynamic DNS domain names in C2.
TA2541 has used dynamic DNS services for C2 infrastructure.

techniques.name: Fast Flux DNS
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use Fast Flux DNS to hide a command and control channel behind an array of rapidly changing IP addresses linked to a single domain resolution.

procedures.text: Amadey has used fast flux DNS for its C2.
menuPass has used dynamic DNS service providers to host malicious domains.
TA505 has used fast flux to mask botnets by distributing payloads across multiple IPs.
gh0st RAT operators have used dynamic DNS to mask the true location of their C2 behind rapidly changing IP addresses.

techniques.name: Domain Generation Algorithms
techniques.summary: Adversaries may make use of Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) to dynamically identify a destination domain for command and control traffic rather than relying on a list of static IP addresses or domains.

procedures.text: Aria-body has the ability to use a DGA for C2 communications.
AsyncRAT use a DGA to generate a C2 domains.
QakBot can use domain generation algorithms in C2 communication.
Doki has used the DynDNS service and a DGA based on the Dogecoin blockchain to generate C2 domains.

techniques.name: DNS Calculation
techniques.summary: Adversaries may perform calculations on addresses returned in DNS results to determine which port and IP address to use for command and control, rather than relying on a predetermined port number or the actual returne...

procedures.text: APT12 has used multiple variants of DNS Calculation including multiplying the first two octets of an IP address and adding the third octet to that value in order to get a resulting command and control port.

techniques.name: System Services
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse system services or daemons to execute commands or programs. Adversaries can execute malicious content by interacting with or creating services either locally or remotely.

procedures.text: Salt Typhoon has utilized SNMP daemon to execute commands to include SNMPwalk.

techniques.name: Launchctl
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse launchctl to execute commands or programs. Launchctl interfaces with launchd, the service management framework for macOS.

procedures.text: LoudMiner launched the QEMU services in the /Library/LaunchDaemons/ folder using launchctl . It also uses launchctl to unload all Launch Daemons when updating to a newer version of LoudMiner.
Cuckoo Stealer can use `launchctl` to load a LaunchAgent for persistence.
AppleJeus has loaded a plist file using the launchctl command.
macOS.OSAMiner has used `launchctl` to restart the Launch Agent.

techniques.name: Service Execution
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse the Windows service control manager to execute malicious commands or payloads. The Windows service control manager ( services.exe ) is an interface to manage and manipulate services.

procedures.text: Pupy uses PsExec to execute a payload or commands on a remote host.
DarkGate tries to elevate privileges to SYSTEM using PsExec to locally execute as a service, such as cmd /c c:\temp\PsExec.exe -accepteula -j -d -s [Target Binary] .
Cobalt Strike can use PsExec to execute a payload on a remote host. It can also use Service Control Manager to start new services.
Vidar has resumed the suspended process RegAsm.exe.

techniques.name: Systemctl
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse systemctl to execute commands or programs. Systemctl is the primary interface for systemd, the Linux init system and service manager.

procedures.text: TeamTNT has created system services to execute cryptocurrency mining software.
CanisterWorm has used executed `systemctl --user daemon-reload` to reload systemd, then enables and starts the malicious service.

techniques.name: Lateral Tool Transfer
techniques.summary: Adversaries may transfer tools or other files between systems in a compromised environment.

procedures.text: Medusa Group has utilized legitimate software services such as PDQ Deploy to transfer malicious binaries and tools to other victimized hosts within the target environment.
Emotet has copied itself to remote systems using the `service.exe` filename.
INC Ransomware can push its encryption executable to multiple endpoints within compromised infrastructure.
BlackCat can replicate itself across connected servers via `psexec`.

techniques.name: Non-Standard Port
techniques.summary: Adversaries may communicate using a protocol and port pairing that are typically not associated. For example, HTTPS over port 8088 or port 587 as opposed to the traditional port 443.

procedures.text: WIRTE has used HTTPS over ports 2083 and 2087 for C2.
Hannotog uses non-standard listening ports, such as UDP 5900, for command and control purposes.
Silence has used port 444 when sending data about the system from the client to the server.
PingPull can use HTTPS over port 8080 for C2.

techniques.name: Protocol Tunneling
techniques.summary: Adversaries may tunnel network communications to and from a victim system within a separate protocol to avoid detection/network filtering and/or enable access to otherwise unreachable systems.

procedures.text: Neo-reGeorg can tunnel data in and out of targeted networks.
FIN13 has utilized web shells and Java tools for tunneling capabilities to and from compromised assets.
Heyoka Backdoor can use spoofed DNS requests to create a bidirectional tunnel between a compromised host and its C2 servers.
Magic Hound has used Plink to tunnel RDP over SSH.

techniques.name: Encrypted Channel
techniques.summary: Adversaries may employ an encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol.

procedures.text: RCSession can use an encrypted beacon to check in with C2.
Cryptoistic can engage in encrypted communications with C2.
Gomir uses a custom encryption algorithm for content sent to command and control infrastructure.
Chaes has used encryption for its C2 channel.

techniques.name: Symmetric Cryptography
techniques.summary: Adversaries may employ a known symmetric encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol.

procedures.text: Dridex has encrypted traffic with RC4.
SMOKEDHAM has encrypted its C2 traffic with RC4.
InvisiMole uses variations of a simple XOR encryption routine for C&C communications.
StarProxy has leveraged two 256-byte XOR keys to encrypt and decrypt network packets using a custom algorithm.

techniques.name: Asymmetric Cryptography
techniques.summary: Adversaries may employ a known asymmetric encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol.

procedures.text: SombRAT can SSL encrypt C2 traffic.
Uroburos has used a combination of a Diffie-Hellman key exchange mixed with a pre-shared key (PSK) to encrypt its top layer of C2 communications.

Cyclops Blink can encrypt C2 messages with AES-256-CBC sent underneath TLS. OpenSSL library functions are also used to encrypt each message using a randomly generated key and IV, which are then encrypted using a hard-coded RSA public key.
REPTILE can use TLS over raw TCP for secure C2.

techniques.name: Hijack Execution Flow
techniques.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the way operating systems run programs.

procedures.text: DarkGate edits the Registry key HKCU\Software\Classes\mscfile\shell\open\command to execute a malicious AutoIt script. When eventvwr.exe is executed, this will call the Microsoft Management Console (mmc.exe), which in turn references the...
One of Dtrack can replace the normal flow of a program execution with malicious code.
SPAWNCHIMERA can persist across system upgrades by hijacking the execution flow of dspkginstall, a binary used during the system upgrade process.
ShimRat can hijack the cryptbase.dll within migwiz.exe to escalate privileges and bypass UAC controls.

techniques.name: DLL
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse dynamic-link library files (DLLs) in order to achieve persistence, escalate privileges, and evade defenses.

procedures.text: Chimera has used side loading to place malicious DLLs in memory.
Cinnamon Tempest has used search order hijacking to launch Cobalt Strike Beacons. Cinnamon Tempest has also abused legitimate executables to side-load weaponized DLLs.
Chinoxy can use a digitally signed binary ("Logitech Bluetooth Wizard Host Process") to load its dll into memory.
MuddyWater maintains persistence on victim networks through side-loading dlls to trick legitimate programs into running malware.

techniques.name: Dylib Hijacking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may execute their own payloads by placing a malicious dynamic library (dylib) with an expected name in a path a victim application searches at runtime.

procedures.text: Empire has a dylib hijacker module that generates a malicious dylib given the path to a legitimate dylib of a vulnerable application.

techniques.name: Executable Installer File Permissions Weakness
techniques.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the binaries used by an installer. These processes may automatically execute specific binaries as part of their functionality or to perform other actions.

procedures.text: Mustang Panda has leveraged legitimate software installer executables such as Setup Factory “IRSetup.exe” to drop and execute their payload.

techniques.name: Dynamic Linker Hijacking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking environment variables the dynamic linker uses to load shared libraries.

procedures.text: Aquatic Panda modified the ld.so preload file in Linux environments to enable persistence for Winnti malware.
Rocke has modified /etc/ld.so.preload to hook libc functions in order to hide the installed dropper and mining software in process lists.
Hildegard has modified /etc/ld.so.preload to intercept shared library import functions.
HiddenWasp adds itself as a shared object to the LD_PRELOAD environment variable.

techniques.name: Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable
techniques.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking environment variables used to load libraries.

procedures.text: PowerSploit contains a collection of Privesc-PowerUp modules that can discover and exploit path interception opportunities in the PATH environment variable.
BRICKSTORM has checked hard-coded paths of `/etc/sysconfig/` or `/etc/sysconfig/network` prior to execution and loading file contents from that path.
Empire contains modules that can discover and exploit path interception opportunities in the PATH environment variable.

DarkGate overrides the %windir% environment variable by setting a Registry key, HKEY_CURRENT_User\Environment\windir , to an alternate command to execute a malicious AutoIt script. This allows DarkGate to run every time the scheduled tas...

techniques.name: Path Interception by Search Order Hijacking
techniques.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the search order used to load other programs.

procedures.text: Empire contains modules that can discover and exploit search order hijacking vulnerabilities.
PowerSploit contains a collection of Privesc-PowerUp modules that can discover and exploit search order hijacking vulnerabilities.

techniques.name: Path Interception by Unquoted Path
techniques.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking vulnerable file path references.

procedures.text: PowerSploit contains a collection of Privesc-PowerUp modules that can discover and exploit unquoted path vulnerabilities.
Empire contains modules that can discover and exploit unquoted path vulnerabilities.

techniques.name: Services File Permissions Weakness
techniques.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the binaries used by services. Adversaries may use flaws in the permissions of Windows services to replace the binary that is executed upon service start.

procedures.text: One variant of BlackEnergy locates existing driver services that have been disabled and drops its driver component into one of those service's paths, replacing the legitimate executable. The malware then sets the hijacked service to star...

techniques.name: Services Registry Permissions Weakness
techniques.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the Registry entries used by services.

techniques.name: COR_PROFILER
techniques.summary: Adversaries may leverage the COR_PROFILER environment variable to hijack the execution flow of programs that load the .NET CLR.

procedures.text: Blue Mockingbird has used wmic.exe and Windows Registry modifications to set the COR_PROFILER environment variable to execute a malicious DLL whenever a process loads the .NET CLR.
DarkTortilla can detect profilers by verifying the `COR_ENABLE_PROFILING` environment variable is present and active.

techniques.name: KernelCallbackTable
techniques.summary: Adversaries may abuse the KernelCallbackTable of a process to hijack its execution flow in order to run their own payloads.

procedures.text: Lazarus Group has abused the KernelCallbackTable to hijack process control flow and execute shellcode.
FinFisher has used the KernelCallbackTable to hijack the execution flow of a process by replacing the __fnDWORD function with the address of a created Asynchronous Procedure Call stub routine.

techniques.name: AppDomainManager
techniques.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking how the .NET `AppDomainManager` loads assemblies.

procedures.text: NIMBUS MANTICORE has leveraged AppDomain Hijacking facilitated through a trojanized `.config` file.
IMAPLoader is executed via the AppDomainManager injection technique.

techniques.name: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure
techniques.summary: An adversary may attempt to modify a cloud account's compute service infrastructure to evade defenses.

techniques.name: Create Snapshot
techniques.summary: An adversary may create a snapshot or data backup within a cloud account to evade defenses.

procedures.text: Pacu can create snapshots of EBS volumes and RDS instances.

techniques.name: Create Cloud Instance
techniques.summary: An adversary may create a new instance or virtual machine (VM) within the compute service of a cloud account to evade defenses.

procedures.text: LAPSUS$ has created new virtual machines within the target's cloud environment after leveraging credential access to cloud assets.
Scattered Spider has created Amazon EC2 instances within the victim's environment.

techniques.name: Delete Cloud Instance
techniques.summary: An adversary may delete a cloud instance after they have performed malicious activities in an attempt to evade detection and remove evidence of their presence.

procedures.text: LAPSUS$ has deleted the target's systems and resources in the cloud to trigger the organization's incident and crisis response process.
Storm-0501 has conducted mass deletion of cloud data stores and resources from Azure subscriptions.

techniques.name: Revert Cloud Instance
techniques.summary: An adversary may revert changes made to a cloud instance after they have performed malicious activities in attempt to evade detection and remove evidence of their presence.

techniques.name: Modify Cloud Compute Configurations
techniques.summary: Adversaries may modify settings that directly affect the size, locations, and resources available to cloud compute infrastructure in order to evade defenses.

techniques.name: Cloud Infrastructure Discovery
techniques.summary: An adversary may attempt to discover infrastructure and resources that are available within an infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) environment.

procedures.text: TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has the ability to search for generic GitHub runners.

Scattered Spider enumerates cloud environments including Amazon Web Services (AWS) S3 buckets to identify server and backup management infrastructure, resource access, databases and storage containers .
TruffleHog can enumerate AWS Infrastructure to include EC2 instances.
ShinyHunters has used Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) Browser and WinSCP to collect information on S3 bucket configurations.

techniques.name: Acquire Infrastructure
techniques.summary: Adversaries may buy, lease, rent, or obtain infrastructure that can be used during targeting. A wide variety of infrastructure exists for hosting and orchestrating adversary operations.

procedures.text: Kimsuky has used funds from stolen and laundered cryptocurrency to acquire operational infrastructure.
Sea Turtle accessed victim networks from VPN service provider networks.
Ember Bear uses services such as IVPN, SurfShark, and Tor to add anonymization to operations.
Indrik Spider has purchased access to victim VPNs to facilitate access to victim environments.

techniques.name: Domains
techniques.summary: Adversaries may acquire domains that can be used during targeting. Domain names are the human readable names used to represent one or more IP addresses.

procedures.text: APT28 registered domains imitating NATO, OSCE security websites, Caucasus information resources, and other organizations.
TA505 has registered domains to impersonate services such as Dropbox to distribute malware.
APT-C-36 has acquired domains to host malicious payloads.

TeamPCP has registered domains resembling legitimate victim sites such as scan.aquasecurtiy[.]org, checkmarx[.]zone, and git-tanstack[.]com to mask C2 and exfiltration endpoints. TeamPCP has also set up a dark web leak site to post stole...

techniques.name: DNS Server
techniques.summary: Adversaries may set up their own Domain Name System (DNS) servers that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Sea Turtle built adversary-in-the-middle DNS servers to impersonate legitimate services that were later used to capture credentials.
Axiom has acquired dynamic DNS services for use in the targeting of intended victims.
HEXANE has set up custom DNS servers to send commands to compromised hosts via TXT records.

techniques.name: Virtual Private Server
techniques.summary: Adversaries may rent Virtual Private Servers (VPSs) that can be used during targeting. There exist a variety of cloud service providers that will sell virtual machines/containers as a service.

procedures.text: Gamaredon Group has used VPS hosting providers for infrastructure outside of Russia.
APT28 hosted phishing domains on free services for brief periods of time during campaigns.
Ember Bear has used virtual private servers (VPSs) to host tools, perform reconnaissance, exploit victim infrastructure, and as a destination for data exfiltration.
LAPSUS$ has used VPS hosting providers for infrastructure.

techniques.name: Server
techniques.summary: Adversaries may buy, lease, rent, or obtain physical servers that can be used during targeting. Use of servers allows an adversary to stage, launch, and execute an operation.

procedures.text: GALLIUM has used Taiwan-based servers that appear to be exclusive to GALLIUM.
Kimsuky has purchased hosting servers with virtual currency and prepaid cards.
Sandworm Team has leased servers from resellers instead of leasing infrastructure directly from hosting companies to enable its operations.
VOID MANTICORE has leveraged backend servers within Iran.

techniques.name: Botnet
techniques.summary: Adversaries may buy, lease, or rent a network of compromised systems that can be used during targeting. A botnet is a network of compromised systems that can be instructed to perform coordinated tasks.

procedures.text: HAFNIUM has incorporated leased devices into covert networks to obfuscate communications.
APT5 has acquired a network of compromised systems – specifically an ORB (operational relay box) network – for follow on activities.
Ke3chang has utilized an ORB (operational relay box) network for reconnaissance and vulnerability exploitation.

techniques.name: Web Services
techniques.summary: Adversaries may register for web services that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Earth Lusca has established GitHub accounts to host their malware.
HAFNIUM has acquired web services for use in C2 and exfiltration.

Contagious Interview has used web services such as Dropbox to receive stolen data and Google Drive, Firebase, GitHub, and Telegram to disseminate files. Contagious Interview has also used a cloud platform such as Vercel for C2 operations...
Medusa Group has utilized a file hosting service named filemail[.]com to host a zip file that contained malicious payloads that facilitated follow-on actions.

techniques.name: Serverless
techniques.summary: Adversaries may purchase and configure serverless cloud infrastructure, such as Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda functions, or Google Apps Scripts, that can be used during targeting.

techniques.name: Malvertising
techniques.summary: Adversaries may purchase online advertisements that can be abused to distribute malware to victims.

procedures.text: Mustard Tempest has posted false advertisements including for software packages and browser updates in order to distribute malware.

Raspberry Robin variants have been delivered via malicious advertising items that, when interacted with, download a malicious archive file containing the initial payload, hosted on services such as Discord.

techniques.name: Compromise Infrastructure
techniques.summary: Adversaries may compromise third-party infrastructure that can be used during targeting. Infrastructure solutions include physical or cloud servers, domains, network devices, and third-party web and DNS services.

techniques.name: Domains
techniques.summary: Adversaries may hijack domains and/or subdomains that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Magic Hound has used compromised domains to host links targeted to specific phishing victims.
SideCopy has compromised domains for some of their infrastructure, including for C2 and staging malware.
Transparent Tribe has compromised domains for use in targeted malicious campaigns.
Gootloader has used compromised legitimate domains to as a delivery network for malicious payloads.

techniques.name: DNS Server
techniques.summary: Adversaries may compromise third-party DNS servers that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Sea Turtle modified Name Server (NS) items to refer to Sea Turtle-controlled DNS servers to provide responses for all DNS lookups.
LAPSUS$ has reconfigured a victim's DNS records to actor-controlled domains and websites.

techniques.name: Virtual Private Server
techniques.summary: Adversaries may compromise third-party Virtual Private Servers (VPSs) that can be used during targeting. There exist a variety of cloud service providers that will sell virtual machines/containers as a service.

procedures.text: Volt Typhoon has compromised Virtual Private Servers (VPS) to proxy C2 traffic.
Turla has used the VPS infrastructure of compromised Iranian threat actors.

techniques.name: Server
techniques.summary: Adversaries may compromise third-party servers that can be used during targeting. Use of servers allows an adversary to stage, launch, and execute an operation.

procedures.text: Lazarus Group has compromised servers to stage malicious tools.
Volt Typhoon has used compromised Paessler Router Traffic Grapher (PRTG) servers from other organizations for C2.
Dragonfly has compromised legitimate websites to host C2 and malware modules.
Turla has used compromised servers as infrastructure.

techniques.name: Botnet
techniques.summary: Adversaries may compromise numerous third-party systems to form a botnet that can be used during targeting. A botnet is a network of compromised systems that can be instructed to perform coordinated tasks.

procedures.text: HAFNIUM has used compromised devices in covert networks to obfuscate communications.
Axiom has used large groups of compromised machines for use as proxy nodes.
Sandworm Team has used a large-scale botnet to target Small Office/Home Office (SOHO) network devices.
APT-C-36 has used a botnet management interface to control large numbers of compromised hosts.

techniques.name: Web Services
techniques.summary: Adversaries may compromise access to third-party web services that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Turla has frequently used compromised WordPress sites for C2 infrastructure.
Earth Lusca has compromised Google Drive repositories.
Gootloader can insert malicious scripts to compromise vulnerable content management systems (CMS).
CURIUM has compromised legitimate websites to enable strategic website compromise attacks.

techniques.name: Serverless
techniques.summary: Adversaries may compromise serverless cloud infrastructure, such as Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda functions, or Google Apps Scripts, that can be used during targeting.

techniques.name: Network Devices
techniques.summary: Adversaries may compromise third-party network devices that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Salt Typhoon has leveraged compromised routers to facilitate operations.
Volt Typhoon has compromised small office and home office (SOHO) network edge devices, many of which were located in the same geographic area as the victim, to proxy network traffic.
APT28 compromised Ubiquiti network devices to act as collection devices for credentials compromised via phishing webpages.
ZIRCONIUM has compromised network devices such as small office and home office (SOHO) routers and IoT devices for ORB (operational relay box) Proxy networks.

techniques.name: Establish Accounts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create and cultivate accounts with services that can be used during targeting. Adversaries can create accounts that can be used to build a persona to further operations.

procedures.text: Contagious Interview has created and maintained personas on code repositories to distribute malicious payloads.
Fox Kitten has created KeyBase accounts to communicate with ransomware victims.
Kimsuky has leveraged stolen PII to create accounts.
Ember Bear has created accounts on dark web forums to obtain various tools and malware.

techniques.name: Social Media Accounts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create and cultivate social media accounts that can be used during targeting. Adversaries can create social media accounts that can be used to build a persona to further operations.

procedures.text: Sandworm Team has established social media accounts to disseminate victim internal-only documents and other sensitive data.
Scattered Spider has created matching fake social media profiles to support new accounts created in victim environments.
Medusa Group has created social media accounts including Telegram and X to publicize their activities.
EXOTIC LILY has established social media profiles to mimic employees of targeted companies.

techniques.name: Email Accounts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create email accounts that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Kimsuky has created email accounts for phishing operations.
Moonstone Sleet has created email accounts to interact with victims, including for phishing purposes.
Magic Hound has established email accounts using fake personas for spearphishing operations.
ShinyHunters has established multiple email accounts, such as shinycorp@tutonota[.]com, for use in extortion activities.

techniques.name: Cloud Accounts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create accounts with cloud providers that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Storm-1811 has created malicious accounts to enable activity via Microsoft Teams, typically spoofing various IT support and helpdesk themes.

techniques.name: Compromise Accounts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may compromise accounts with services that can be used during targeting. For operations incorporating social engineering, the utilization of an online persona may be important.

techniques.name: Social Media Accounts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may compromise social media accounts that can be used during targeting. For operations incorporating social engineering, the utilization of an online persona may be important.

procedures.text: Sandworm Team creates credential capture webpages to compromise existing, legitimate social media accounts.
Leviathan has compromised social media accounts to conduct social engineering attacks.

techniques.name: Email Accounts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may compromise email accounts that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: APT28 has used compromised email accounts to send credential phishing emails.
Magic Hound has compromised personal email accounts through the use of legitimate credentials and gathered additional victim information.
Mustang Panda has compromised legitimate email accounts to use in their spear-phishing operations.
OilRig has compromised email accounts to send phishing emails.

techniques.name: Cloud Accounts
techniques.summary: Adversaries may compromise cloud accounts that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: APT29 has used residential proxies, including Azure Virtual Machines, to obfuscate their access to victim environments.
APT38 has used virtual private server (VPS) providers to host C2 infrastructure including Hostwinds.
APT-C-36 has used compromised Google Drive accounts including one associated with a Colombian government organization.

techniques.name: Develop Capabilities
techniques.summary: Adversaries may build capabilities that can be used during targeting. Rather than purchasing, freely downloading, or stealing capabilities, adversaries may develop their own capabilities in-house.

procedures.text: Kimsuky created and used a mailing toolkit to use in spearphishing attacks.
Contagious Interview developed malicious NPM packages for delivery to or retrieval by victims.
Salt Typhoon has hosted and attended formal training programs for foreign-made IT products to include Cisco Network Academy.
Moonstone Sleet developed malicious npm packages for delivery to or retrieval by victims.

techniques.name: Malware
techniques.summary: Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Kimsuky has developed its own unique malware such as MailFetch.py for use in operations.
FIN13 has utilized custom malware to maintain persistence in a compromised environment.
Moonstone Sleet has developed custom malware, including a malware delivery mechanism masquerading as a legitimate game.
Indrik Spider has developed malware for their operations, including ransomware such as BitPaymer and WastedLocker.

techniques.name: Code Signing Certificates
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create self-signed code signing certificates that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Daggerfly created code signing certificates to sign malicious macOS files.
PROMETHIUM has created self-signed certificates to sign malicious installers.
Patchwork has created self-signed certificates from fictitious and spoofed legitimate software companies that were later used to sign malware.

techniques.name: Digital Certificates
techniques.summary: Adversaries may create self-signed SSL/TLS certificates that can be used during targeting. SSL/TLS certificates are designed to instill trust.

procedures.text: APT29 has created self-signed digital certificates to enable mutual TLS authentication for malware.
PROMETHIUM has created self-signed digital certificates for use in HTTPS C2 traffic.
Gamaredon Group has used the same TLS certificate across its infrastructure.
Storm-0501 has utilized their own self-signed TLS certificate “Microsoft IT TLS CA 5” with their infrastructure.

techniques.name: Exploits
techniques.summary: Adversaries may develop exploits that can be used during targeting. An exploit takes advantage of a bug or vulnerability in order to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior to occur on computer hardware or software.

procedures.text: Volt Typhoon has exploited zero-day vulnerabilities for initial access.
UNC3886 has used zero-day vulnerabilities CVE-2022-41328 against FortiOS and CVE-2023-20867 and CVE-2023-34048 against VMware vCenter.
Leviathan has rapidly transformed and adapted public exploit proof-of-concept code for new vulnerabilities and utilized them against target networks.
ShinyHunters has exploited zero-day vulnerability CVE-2026-35273 against Oracle PeopleSoft application infrastructure.

techniques.name: Obtain Capabilities
techniques.summary: Adversaries may buy and/or steal capabilities that can be used during targeting. Rather than developing their own capabilities in-house, adversaries may purchase, freely download, or steal them.

techniques.name: Malware
techniques.summary: Adversaries may buy, steal, or download malware that can be used during targeting. Malicious software can include payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors, packers, and C2 protocols.

procedures.text: LuminousMoth has obtained and used malware such as Cobalt Strike.
MuddyWater has used publicly available malware for operations, likely to blend in with other cybercriminals.
TA2541 has used multiple strains of malware available for purchase on criminal forums or in open-source repositories.
APT-C-36 has utilized well known malware including the Packer-as-a-Service HeartCrypt, PureCrypter, and open-source RATs such as Remcos.

techniques.name: Tool
techniques.summary: Adversaries may buy, steal, or download software tools that can be used during targeting. Tools can be open or closed source, free or commercial.

procedures.text: DarkVishnya has obtained and used tools such as Impacket, Winexe, and PsExec.
Turla has obtained and customized publicly-available tools like Mimikatz.
Inception has obtained and used open-source tools such as LaZagne.
Magic Hound has obtained and used tools like Havij, sqlmap, Metasploit, Mimikatz, and Plink.

techniques.name: Code Signing Certificates
techniques.summary: Adversaries may buy and/or steal code signing certificates that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Wizard Spider has obtained code signing certificates signed by DigiCert, GlobalSign, and COMOOD for malware payloads.
OilRig has obtained stolen code signing certificates to digitally sign malware.
BlackTech has used stolen code-signing certificates for its malicious payloads.
FIN8 has used an expired open-source X.509 certificate for testing in the OpenSSL repository, to connect to actor-controlled C2 servers.

techniques.name: Digital Certificates
techniques.summary: Adversaries may buy and/or steal SSL/TLS certificates that can be used during targeting. SSL/TLS certificates are designed to instill trust.

procedures.text: Silent Librarian has obtained free Let's Encrypt SSL certificates for use on their phishing pages.
Lazarus Group has obtained SSL certificates for their C2 domains.

Sea Turtle created new certificates using a technique called the actors performed "certificate impersonation," a technique in which Sea Turtle obtained a certificate authority-signed X.509 certificate from another provider for the same d...
Mustang Panda has obtained SSL certificates for their C2 domains.

techniques.name: Exploits
techniques.summary: Adversaries may buy, steal, or download exploits that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Ember Bear has obtained exploitation scripts against publicly-disclosed vulnerabilities from public repositories.
Kimsuky has obtained exploit code for various CVEs.
Salt Typhoon has obtained and utilized numerous exploits that target network edge devices to include Cisco IOS, Palo Alto Pan-OS Global Protect, and Ivanti Connect Secure.

techniques.name: Vulnerabilities
techniques.summary: Adversaries may acquire information about vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: In 2017, Sandworm Team conducted technical research related to vulnerabilities associated with websites used by the Korean Sport and Olympic Committee, a Korean power company, and a Korean airport.
Volt Typhoon has used publicly available exploit code for initial access.

Storm-0501 has obtained capabilities to exploit N-day vulnerabilities associated with public facing services to gain initial access to victim environments to include Zoho ManageEngine (CVE-2022-47966), Citrix NetScaler “Citrix Bleed” (CV...

techniques.name: Artificial Intelligence
techniques.summary: Adversaries may obtain access to generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as large language models (LLMs), to aid various techniques during targeting.

procedures.text: NIMBUS MANTICORE has appeared to have leveraged AI to assist in malware generation due to coding patterns and modular code organization.
Contagious Interview has appeared to have used AI to generate images and content to facilitate their campaigns.
ShinyHunters has used Bland AI to create conversational pathways tailored to specific scenarios during voice phishing attacks.
LazyWiper is believed to have been generated by a large language model (LLM) due to the non-sensical comments in the code.

techniques.name: Gather Victim Identity Information
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's identity that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: LAPSUS$ has gathered detailed information of target employees to enhance their social engineering lures.
HEXANE has identified specific potential victims at targeted organizations.
VOID MANTICORE has gathered details on their intended victims to aid in social engineering efforts for leveraging tailored themes of attacks.
Scattered Spider has used information from previous data breaches to identify employee names to be used in social engineering.

techniques.name: Credentials
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather credentials that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: APT28 has harvested user's login credentials.

Magic Hound gathered credentials from two victims that they then attempted to validate across 75 different websites. Magic Hound has also collected credentials from over 900 Fortinet VPN servers in the US, Europe, and Israel.
Leviathan has collected compromised credentials to use for targeting efforts.
LAPSUS$ has gathered user identities and credentials to gain initial access to a victim's organization; the group has also called an organization's help desk to reset a target's credentials.

techniques.name: Email Addresses
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather email addresses that can be used during targeting. Even if internal instances exist, organizations may have public-facing email infrastructure and addresses for employees.

procedures.text: Saint Bear gathered victim email information in advance of phishing operations for targeted attacks.
Moonstone Sleet gathered victim email address information for follow-on phishing activity.
TA551 has used spoofed company emails that were acquired from email clients on previously infected hosts to target other individuals.
Volt Typhoon has targeted the personal emails of key network and IT staff at victim organizations.

techniques.name: Employee Names
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather employee names that can be used during targeting. Employee names be used to derive email addresses as well as to help guide other reconnaissance efforts and/or craft more-believable lures.

procedures.text: Kimsuky has collected victim employee name information.
Sandworm Team's research of potential victim organizations included the identification and collection of employee information.
Silent Librarian has collected lists of names for individuals from targeted organizations.

techniques.name: Gather Victim Network Information
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's networks that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Volt Typhoon has conducted extensive pre-compromise reconnaissance to learn about the target organization’s network.

Indrik Spider has downloaded tools, such as the Advanced Port Scanner utility and Lansweeper, to conduct internal reconnaissance of the victim network. Indrik Spider has also accessed the victim’s VMware VCenter, which had information ab...
HAFNIUM gathered the fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) for targeted Exchange servers in the victim's environment.

techniques.name: Domain Properties
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's network domain(s) that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Sandworm Team conducted technical reconnaissance of the Parliament of Georgia's official internet domain prior to its 2019 attack.
AADInternals can gather information about a tenant’s domains using public Microsoft APIs.

techniques.name: DNS
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's DNS that can be used during targeting.

techniques.name: Network Trust Dependencies
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's network trust dependencies that can be used during targeting.

techniques.name: Network Topology
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's network topology that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Salt Typhoon has used configuration files from exploited network devices to help discover upstream and downstream network segments.
MuddyWater has mapped target networks; access to this information and more is then shared/sold to other Iran threat actors.
FIN13 has searched for infrastructure that can provide remote access to an environment for targeting efforts.
Volt Typhoon has conducted extensive reconnaissance of victim networks including identifying network topologies.

techniques.name: IP Addresses
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather the victim's IP addresses that can be used during targeting. Public IP addresses may be allocated to organizations by block, or a range of sequential addresses.

procedures.text: Andariel has limited its watering hole attacks to specific IP address ranges.
Magic Hound has captured the IP addresses of visitors to their phishing sites.
HAFNIUM has obtained IP addresses for publicly-accessible Exchange servers.

techniques.name: Network Security Appliances
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's network security appliances that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Volt Typhoon has identified target network security measures as part of pre-compromise reconnaissance.

techniques.name: Gather Victim Org Information
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's organization that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: APT28 has used large language models (LLMs) to gather information about satellite capabilities.
MirrorFace has placed specific content in phishing emails to target members of particular political parties.
Lazarus Group has studied publicly available information about a targeted organization to tailor spearphishing efforts against specific departments and/or individuals.
Moonstone Sleet has gathered information on victim organizations through email and social media interaction.

techniques.name: Determine Physical Locations
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather the victim's physical location(s) that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Magic Hound has collected location information from visitors to their phishing sites.

techniques.name: Business Relationships
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's business relationships that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Dragonfly has collected open source information to identify relationships between organizations for targeting purposes.
LAPSUS$ has gathered detailed knowledge of an organization's supply chain relationships.
In preparation for its attack against the 2018 Winter Olympics, Sandworm Team conducted online research of partner organizations listed on an official PyeongChang Olympics partnership site.

techniques.name: Identify Business Tempo
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's business tempo that can be used during targeting.

techniques.name: Identify Roles
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about identities and roles within the victim organization that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Volt Typhoon has identified key network and IT staff members pre-compromise at targeted organizations.
LAPSUS$ has gathered detailed knowledge of team structures within a target organization.
FIN7 has identified IT staff and employees who had higher levels of administrative rights.
HEXANE has identified executives, HR, and IT staff at victim organizations for further targeting.

techniques.name: Gather Victim Host Information
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's hosts that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Volt Typhoon has conducted pre-compromise reconnaissance for victim host information.

techniques.name: Hardware
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's host hardware that can be used during targeting.

techniques.name: Software
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's host software that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Magic Hound has captured the user-agent strings from visitors to their phishing sites.

Sandworm Team has researched software code to enable supply-chain operations, most notably for the 2017 NotPetya attack. Sandworm Team also collected a list of computers using specific software as part of its targeting efforts.
Andariel has inserted a malicious script within compromised websites to collect potential victim information such as browser type, system language, Flash Player version, and other data.

techniques.name: Firmware
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's host firmware that can be used during targeting.

techniques.name: Client Configurations
techniques.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's client configurations that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: HAFNIUM has interacted with Office 365 tenants to gather details regarding target's environments.

techniques.name: Search Open Websites/Domains
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search freely available websites and/or domains for information about victims that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Mustang Panda has used open-source research to identify information about victims to use in targeting to include creating weaponized phishing lures and attachments.
Volt Typhoon has conducted pre-compromise web searches for victim information.
Contagious Interview has utilized open-source indicator of compromise repositories to determine their exposure to include VirusTotal, and MalTrail.
APT-C-36 has gathered information on Colombian financial institutions, including Bancolombia, BBVA, Banco Caja Social, and Davivienda to craft phishing pages.

techniques.name: Social Media
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search social media for information about victims that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Kimsuky has used Twitter to monitor potential victims and to prepare targeted phishing e-mails.
Contagious Interview had identified and solicited victims through social media such as LinkedIn, X, and Telegram.
EXOTIC LILY has copied data from social media sites to impersonate targeted individuals.

techniques.name: Search Engines
techniques.summary: Adversaries may use search engines to collect information about victims that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Kimsuky has searched for vulnerabilities, tools, and geopolitical trends on Google to target victims.

techniques.name: Code Repositories
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search public code repositories for information about victims that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Contagious Interview had identified and solicited victims through code repositories such as GitHub.
LAPSUS$ has searched public code repositories for exposed credentials.
HAFNIUM has discovered leaked corporate credentials on public repositories including GitHub.

Shai-Hulud has the ability to search open sites and code repositories for compromised credentials. Shai-Hulud has discovered packages associated with compromised accounts. Shai-Hulud has also searched code repositories for other compromi...

techniques.name: Search Victim-Owned Websites
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search websites owned by the victim for information that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Silent Librarian has searched victim's websites to identify the interests and academic areas of targeted individuals and to scrape source code, branding, and organizational contact information for phishing pages.
Kimsuky has searched for information on the target company's website.
Volt Typhoon has conducted pre-compromise reconnaissance on victim-owned sites.
EXOTIC LILY has used contact forms on victim websites to generate phishing e-mails.

techniques.name: Active Scanning
techniques.summary: Adversaries may execute active reconnaissance scans to gather information that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Salt Typhoon has scanned victim environments for open ports and services.

techniques.name: Scanning IP Blocks
techniques.summary: Adversaries may scan victim IP blocks to gather information that can be used during targeting. Public IP addresses may be allocated to organizations by block, or a range of sequential addresses.

procedures.text: Ember Bear has targeted IP ranges for vulnerability scanning related to government and critical infrastructure organizations.
TeamTNT has scanned specific lists of target IP addresses.

techniques.name: Vulnerability Scanning
techniques.summary: Adversaries may scan victims for vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: Sandworm Team has scanned network infrastructure for vulnerabilities as part of its operational planning.
Volatile Cedar has performed vulnerability scans of the target server.
Leviathan has conducted reconnaissance against target networks of interest looking for vulnerable, end-of-life, or no longer maintainted devices against which to rapidly deploy exploits.
Ember Bear has used publicly available tools such as MASSCAN and Acunetix for vulnerability scanning of public-facing infrastructure.

techniques.name: Wordlist Scanning
techniques.summary: Adversaries may iteratively probe infrastructure using brute-forcing and crawling techniques.

procedures.text: APT41 leverages various tools and frameworks to brute-force directories on web servers.
Volatile Cedar has used DirBuster and GoBuster to brute force web directories and DNS subdomains.

techniques.name: Search Open Technical Databases
techniques.summary: Adversaries may search freely available technical databases for information about victims that can be used during targeting.

procedures.text: APT28 has used large language models (LLMs) to assist in script development and deployment.
Kimsuky has used LLMs to better understand publicly reported vulnerabilities.
